He said. Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few brief words on the situation facing Canadian grain producers. I would then like to make some comments on the Bill itself.
I do not think it is any secret that international grain prices are extremely depressed. If one considers what has been happening around the world, one realizes that there is an excess amount of product over what has come to be called real demand". If one looks at the producing countries which are causing the problem, one will see, at least in my view, that it is being caused by the European community. Through its agricultural policy the European community has been subsidizing agriculture significantly since the Treaty of Rome.
As a result of not placing any limits on over-all production, very large subsidies have caused production to increase dramatically. Not only have levels been very much of an incentive to production, but the fact that prices paid to producers in Europe have been constant has also been an incentive to produce. Any businessman or farmer knows that if one can plan on a year-by-year basis on certainty of prices, then that in itself, as well as the fact that one does not have to be concerned about varying prices, is an incentive to production. If we consider the over-all level of prices and the price support system which the Europeans have in place, we will see that that price level is also a very substantial incentive to producers in Europe to increase their over-all production.
I would now like to provide Hon. Members with two examples of this which I think make the point. If we consider the southern Prairies in our country, we see that we produce very high quality Durum wheat. It is probably second to none in the world. It is recognized around the world as being of very high quality. In the current crop year, our producers are receiving $130 per tonne as an initial payment. European producers are receiving $480 per tonne, over three times what the Canadian producer is receiving. If we do our arithmetic and translate that figure into Canadian dollars, we see that the Europeans are receiving about $13 a bushel for Durum wheat.
In terms of the barley market internationally, Europeans are one of our major competitors. They produce considerable quantities of barley for export. Presently, our producers are receiving $80 per tonne as an initial payment. If we look to what is happening in Europe, we see that European prices are over three times what the Canadian producers are receiving. The Europeans are receiving $285 per tonne. The price varies from time to time, but that is the general level. So when we compare $80 per tonne to $285 per tonne, we see that that is a very attractive price as compared to what Canadian producers are receiving.
With respect to other commodities, almost every agricultural commodity that Europe produces is now in a surplus position. For example, with respect to beef, Canada has a high quality beef herd. As far as Canadian beef producers are concerned, there is probably a gene pool in terms of Canadian beef which is second to none around the world. If we consider Europe, we see that through incentives to production Europe has gone from being a net importer of something in the order of 300,000 tonnes of beef in 1978 to being the largest exporter in 1984. If we consider what Europe exported last year, we see that Europeans exported something in the order of 600,000 tonnes of beef. In addition, they have about 700,000 tonnes of beef in storage, according to the figures that we have seen. That is a tremendous amount of product in storage for which there is no apparent market at the price that the Europeans are paying to produce it.
If we talk about quantity of products, again, we should look at what is happening with respect to wheat. As recently as 1977, just 10 years ago, Europe was a net importer of wheat to the tune of about 24 million tonnes. With respect to last year,
March 5, 1987

as far as Europe is concerned, it was a net exporter of wheat to the tune of close to 15 million tonnes. It has gone in a very short period of time from being a major importer to being a major exporter. In fact, it is now the third largest exporter of wheat in the world after the United States and Canada. I can also talk about Japan in this vein. Japan is another country which protects its agricultural sector from the realities of the world market-place.
This is a very difficult situation that we face. What we have been doing as a Government is to take two deliberate approaches. If we are to find a lasting solution to the problem, it must be found at the international level. This is why Canada has been placing so much emphasis on talks with respect to agricultural products and trade problems internationally. It was our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who at the last summit placed agriculture on the agenda. That is why we have been so concerned about having agriculture form part of the GATT agenda and why we have been so supportive of the GATT process. We have done this so that this time around at the GATT discussions agriculture will be included as a main agenda item. This is why we are pursuing every other international meeting in which we are involved, pursuing it in the sense that we want to have agriculture as part of the discussions because it is a very major problem.
[DOT] (U30)
We also make sure that we sell our grain and oilseeds. Last year Canada increased its world share of the wheat market. In the present crop year we have the prospect of again increasing exports. In order to do that, we are suffering severe price penalties because the price is extremely low. We all know how serious the situation is. We have been attempting to deal with the situation through some direct government involvement. Some Acts have been amended to allow for stabilization money to be made available sooner. The Western Grain Stabilization Act was put through the House two years ago to allow for interim payments under that Act prior to spring seeding. It was supported by all Parties in the House, and it has been well received by producers.
The Government has removed the tax on farm fuel. Under the Special Canadian Grains Program we are at present paying out the largest financial support program in the history of the country, as far as farmers are concerned.
The Bill in front of us provides for cash advances to farmers in the Wheat Board region who have harvested their grain but have not had an opportunity to sell it. This will be of assistance to farmers in providing them cash more quickly than if they had to wait for delivery opportunities and quotas to open up. It will also help the business community because there will be extra cash in circulation prior to the time when grain would normally be sold and when producers would realize the cash from the sale of that grain. This Act was first introduced in 1957. The former Minister of Agriculture under Mr. Diefen-baker, the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), made one of the most interesting speeches I
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
have heard in the House. He talked about the time when he introduced the Act and brought it in.
This Act is being amended today so that producers will be in a position to benefit from it in a more timely and a more easily administered fashion. To state it very briefly, at present the forms for which producers apply each year have to be set by Order in Council. The forms vary little from year to year. The Canadian Wheat Board is the organization that administers this Act. One of the amendments will allow the Board itself to set the prescribed form. It will be simpler in detail, and will allow for less red tape and hold-up.
In the Bill there are also provisions for emergency cash advances for unthreshed grain. In the fall of the year if the harvest is late and the producers have not been able to harvest their grain and receive the cash advance, there are provisions in the Bill to allow for emergency cash advances. One of them is for unthreshed grain, so that the producer can have half of the cash advance if he has grown the grain but has not yet had an opportunity to harvest it by November 15. In this case there will not be an Order in Council required and it can simply be done at the discretion of the Minister of the day. This will speed things up.
We are doing the same thing concerning cash advances for drying tough and damp grain. At present there are provisions in the Act that allow for a $3,000 assistance package and an interest-free cash advance that allow producers to take advantage of that extra loan if they have grain that has been harvested but it is in a tough or damp condition. If there has been a difficult harvest season, this will assist people to dry the grain and get it into marketing condition.
The Hon. Member for Mackenzie (Mr. Scowen), who is a registered seed grower, and who is well recognized in his area as a very good farmer, has been concerned about one of the aspects of this Bill. In his area of northern Saskatchewan, which is indicative of the northern Prairies in general, farmers dry grain on a more regular basis than in other parts of the Prairies. The Hon. Member has been concerned that we should take a look at this Bill and try to make use of it to assist producers and to encourage them to dry their grain. This is one of the ways in which to assist producers to get a crop off a little sooner. In many cases in doing so, they will harvest a higher quality product.
Canada is well known for its high quality grain. This amendment will be used to provide the Minister of the day with more discretion to decide when there can be cash advances for drying. That provision will be used on a trial or test basis in northeastern Saskatchewan, covering part of the riding of the Hon. Member for Mackenzie, and probably part of the riding of Prince Albert, to look at doing exactly what the Hon. Member suggested, that is, to make use of cash advances to assist producers to harvest grain in a higher quality condition. In that manner, they will be in a better position to market a better quality product.

March 5, 1987
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
Without the efforts and the insistence of the Hon. Member for Mackenzie, we would not be engaged in this project. We look forward to working with the producers and Members from that area to see how this will work. We will then see the success rate, and on that basis how this measure can be used in other parts of the Prairies.
In addition, we will be able to set the rates of the cash advance in a simpler fashion which will not involve an Order in Council. It will be in the regulations in such a manner that an Order in Council will not be required.
In the Bill, we will also be amending the procedure by which a producer who rents land can obtain a cash advance. At present that producer has to receive a signature from his landlord before he can receive the cash advance. The Advance Payments for Crops Act, which applies to other crops in the Prairies as well as other crops in the rest of the country, has provisions that simplify this, so that there will be less hol'd-up in receiving the cash advance for people who rent land.
The Act is also being amended so that everybody is treated fairly across the country. Nobody will receive a larger cash advance than $30,000. There is some concern that we may be limiting cash advances, because at present producers can receive a cash advance under the Western Grain Advance Payments Act, and they are also eligible for a cash advance under the Advance Payments for Crops Act. One of the amendments limits the total amount of advance that any producer can receive to a maximum of $30,000. In our view, that is a fair and even-handed way to proceed. If there is concern that the cash advances are too low, then we can look at raising the over-all levels so that everybody is treated fairly. The present situation is such that not everybody across the country is eligible for two cash advances, one under the Advance Payments for Crops Act, and one under the present Bill. By limiting the amount to the maximum everybody is treated evenly.
Another amendment concerns people who, because of the fact that they irrigate, grow more grain than other people who farm under dry land conditions. Farmers who irrigated may in fact have enough grain on hand to be able to qualify for the maximum, or certainly a fairly large amount. However, because of the way in which the Act presently sets the amount for which they are eligible on an acre basis, they in fact are not eligible for the full amount for which they should be eligible based upon the amount of grain they have grown, harvested, and stored on their farms.
[DOT] (U40)
One amendment changes that so that the maximum amount a producer is able to receive will be directly related to his production, not to the amount of acres which he farms. That is an improvement and something which everyone welcomes. It treats people in an even-handed way, based upon the amount of production on their farms.
There are two other amendments. I might say that repayment under the Act has been very good, but unfortunately there are cases where producers have gone into default. When they go into default and cannot repay the cash advance, because it is a loan, interest rates are set at the time their loan is declared in default. Let us say some producers went into default four years or five years ago when interest rates were extremely high, from 16 per cent to 20 per cent. Those producers are still paying interest rates at that level, because there is no provision in the present Act to adjust interest rates after they have been initially set.
We are amending the Act to set interest rates yearly, based upon current conditions. Again I think it is a step in the right direction because it treats people on a fair basis. People who have gone into default are having a bad time, obviously, and they do not need to be penalized further in today's situation by having to pay interest rates which are as much as 8 per cent and 10 per cent higher than present interest rates.
Another amendment allows the Canadian Wheat Board, which administers the Act, much more discretion in terms of making adjustments for people who, for one reason or another, have not been able to deliver grain. It can be because of weather conditions, road problems, washed out bridges, personal hardships in their families, or such things. The way the Act is presently written, the Canadian Wheat Board does not have the latitude to make some adjustments based upon common sense or upon an approach which includes information which should be relevant to producers who have had problems in terms of delivering grain and therefore fulfilling their obligations under the Act once they have taken a cash advance.
All in all I think the legislation has worked well. As I said, it has been in effect for almost 30 years. It is one which benefits farmers and local communities served by farmers, because it puts cash into the hands of farmers quicker than would otherwise be the case. The amendments we are discussing today will streamline the administration of the Bill in such a way that the functioning of the Act will be more timely and more responsive to the needs of producers.
In conclusion, we very much appreciate the co-operation from all sides of the House, not only at second reading but during its consideration in committee and here today. I thank the Hon. Member for Mackenzie who made some very useful suggestions. As a result of the amendments before us today, we will be able to look at the concerns he raised and take them into account. We will be able to operate on a trial or experimental basis advances for drying purposes, which will encourage people to harvest their grain and get it off in a more high quality condition than would otherwise be the case.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the third reading debate on Bill C-12. The Minister has given a very good summary of the legislative provisions of the Bill. Unfortunately, he did not answer the $64,000 question about which all farmers in western Canada
March 5, 1987

are concerned, that is, what will be the exact initial price for grain in the coming crop year. I should like to talk a little about that this morning.
However, at the same time I agree with the Hon. Minister that the Bill improves the legislation for cash advances. Many of the amendments are technical in a way, but they provide significant improvement for farmers who utilize this very good Act and its provisions.
My regret is that we did not pass the legislation last October. The Bill was actually brought in on October 7. We debated it first on October 21 and again on October 28. Then it went to committee and did not return until December 3. In fact, if we had been able to pass it in the House on October 21, or if we did not have so many government Members speaking on the Bill on October 28 and so on, the amendments to the legislation could have been available to farmers in this crop year.
As the Minister outlined, the amendments are pretty significant. They are based upon stored grain instead of cash advances on an acreage basis. Farmers who are paying high interest rates due to default on previous cash advances could have had the benefit of a lower interest rate throughout the winter. Farmers who were tenants could have had the advantage of a cash advance rather than being denied it throughout the winter, which was one of the most difficult winters faced by western grain farmers. These provisions would have been extremely beneficial, but I guess they are better late than never. Essentially we miss a whole year of the benefits under the program.
When we first debated the Bill and offered to expedite its passage last October 21,1 do not believe the quotas were open to any extent in most areas of the West, so cash advances would have been very valuable to farmers at that time.
I want to inquire about some of the most devastating news to hit western Canada yesterday. It was indicated that the Canadian Wheat Board recommended that the initial price be reduced by 20 per cent. Just to put that into perspective, two years ago or three years ago the initial price for No. 1 wheat was $170 per tonne. Two years ago it was $160 per tonne. Last year it was $130 per tonne. If the recommendations of the Canadian Wheat Board are acted upon, we will see the initial price for No. 1 wheat being down to $105 per tonne. I do not think any sector of the economy has faced such a devastating blow as to see its gross price drop from $170 per tonne to $105 per tonne. If there is any other such sector, it is perhaps the petroleum sector. That industry has faced a similar kind of reduction in the value of its commodity. Unfortunately, grain, wheat, barley, oats and crude oil are produced essentially in our two western Provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan.
I was surprised yesterday when the Minister seemed to deny the report in the House that the Wheat Board was recommending a 20 per cent reduction in the initial price of wheat.

Clearly the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) was telling those attending the CFA conference in Hull that that was the recommendation. We have had to face the most devastating news two years in a row. There was a 19 per cent reduction in the initial price of wheat last year, and now there is a 20 per cent reduction this year from something around $3 Canadian a bushel Canadian to about $2.50 a bushel or even lower.
There is concern that the Government is not coming clean with Canadians. Perhaps the reason the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is so low in the polls these days is that he does not come clean with Canadians about exactly what the true facts are. In any event, the Minister of Agriculture indicated yesterday, as reported in a Canadian Press story, that farmers should not count on massive Government aid when deciding what to plant this year. That was the devastating news in the Budget.
There was a great deal of talk about the special grains program put in place last fall but which is really only being paid in this fiscal year. There has been nary a word about the new crop year. Do people decide to plant crops this year? Will the price be as low as $2.50 a bushel for No. 1 wheat? You can imagine what the price of barley and the price of No. 3 feed grains will be if the price of No. 1 wheat is as low as that. Why is there no clear indication from the Government about what is to happen?
If we look through the Budget papers, we see no commitment about the new crop year. We do not know whether there will be a special grains program, whether there will be a deficiency payment, whether the existing price for wheat will be maintained, or what is going to be done. The Minister talked about the problems with the EEC and about the price of beef and meat stored by the EEC. However, he did not get into the details on this main agricultural Bill as to what he is going to do about the initial price of wheat this year or whether there will be an additional special grains program. Clearly those questions are on everybody's mind.
We also see that there is no action whatever concerning the farm debt crisis in the Budget papers. Even with a 19 per cent reduction in the price of wheat last year in Saskatchewan and a 17 per cent reduction in the property values-that is an average, it is probably twice that in some areas of the province-there is nary a word in the Budget about new financial assistance relating to the farm debt crisis.
I just had the opportunity a few days ago of looking at the Farm Credit Corporation situation. The FCC is the major federal Government lending agency. It has some 75,000 mortgage accounts across the country. It is interesting to note that 18,000 of these, clearly 25 per cent, are in arrears. Those arrears have grown by 30 per cent in the last 12 months, from January 1986 to January 1987, from $260 million to $377 million. This 30 per cent increase is an increase of $117 million.
The Minister of Agriculture has had a moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation foreclosures in this past year. We are told

March 5, 1987
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
now that some 5,200 of them, or almost one-third of those mortgages in arrears, have been in arrears for more than two years. The FCC's experience is that once mortgages are in arrears for more than two years, it is almost impossible to recoup. That is why we are extremely concerned about there being nothing in the Budget on the farm debt crisis. There is no financial assistance, whether in the form of reduced interests or lower mortgage rates. This is in spite of the reduced price of grain last year. Now we have this double whammy of an increased reduction in price again this year.
I hope we can get a clear pronouncement about where the Government is going on the initial price of grain. But first the Government has to come clean and say that the Wheat Board has recommended a reduction of 20 per cent, if that is what it is. The Minister of Agriculture says that this is what it is. The Minister responsible for the Wheat Board does not say what it is. As a matter of fact, at the CFA meeting yesterday the Minister was surprised because he did not know about that recommendation, and yet members of the advisory board to the Canadian Wheat Board said that this is what was being recommended. We really need a clearer indication of where the Government is going and on what basis a special grains program will be put into effect. I do not think that can be weighted off and negotiated a year from now, next fall or in December. It may not happen at all. There is no election in Saskatchewan this year. If there had been no election last year, it is highly questionable whether there would have been a special grains program.
There are a number of serious problems with the special grains program. People who have switched to alternative crops, peas, lentils and others, to reduce the acreage of wheat are not getting any assistance. I think the Government has to exercise its responsibility, provide leadership and make it clear on what basis there will be assistance and whether there will be assistance, because it is not clear at this time. The Minister heightened that uncertainty when he said yesterday at the Canadian Federation of Agriculture's annual general meeting that farmers should not count on massive government aid when deciding what to plant this year. Here we have the price of wheat going down and probably the prices of all grains going down by 20 per cent perhaps to a price that is even lower in actual dollars than what was paid in the 1930s. Yet the Minister is saying that farmers should not count on any assistance in that regard from the federal Government.
I looked very carefully through the Budget papers to see what assistance would be provided under the Western Grain Stabilization Fund, because that is a major support program. One-third of the money is put in by the farmers and two-thirds by the federal Government. People in the industry have suggested that the fund may be as high as $1 billion this year.
I think it would be useful for the Government, which is not exactly enjoying a lot of popularity in Canada right now, to make it clear how much will be paid out under the Western Grain Stabilization Fund and when it will be paid. Will it be
paid on the basis of two-thirds or 70 per cent in a timely manner in April with the balance in October as it was last year?
In the Budget papers it is suggested that the contribution by the federal Government to the fund in this coming year will be some $99 million. I am told by people from the Department that in fact that fund is about $90 million in the red right now. It is difficult if not impossible to find out exactly how much will be paid out under the Western Grain Stabilization Fund.
I believe there is concern as well with the Government coming clean and outlining exactly what the initial grain price will be. We saw a deficit in the past crop year, 1985-86, of some $201 million, mostly on barley. Some people in the industry have suggested that the deficit in the pool accounts this year will be as high as $400 million to $500 million. Perhaps the Government could spell out exactly what the arrangements on initial price and the special grains or deficiency programs will be. Will it be resource neutral, and on what basis will it be established? It would be very useful to know those things because we will be facing an impossible situation if there is no support or stabilization.
At the Canadian Federation meeting yesterday, I spoke to people from the Saskatchewan and Manitoba pools. They said that many farmers facing a price of $105 per tonne will simply not be able to go to the bank to get the cash flow required to plant this year. I think it is imperative that the Government make it clear what the initial price will be and what kind of stabilization program will be provided.
It seems to me that at this time, farmers are facing greater uncertainty than they have at any time in the past 50 years. In his first three Budgets, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) increased personal taxation by some 50 per cent while dropping back on corporations by 5 per cent. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) has not given any commitment on grain freight rates in the coming year.
We know that the former Minister of Transport, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), was able to instruct the grain transportation agency to reduce its volume from 30.5 million tonnes to 28.5 million tonnes last year. The Prime Minister was therefore able to say at a press conference last April that he had frozen freight rates. Freight rates really were not frozen, the grain transportation agency was simply instructed to reduce its estimate. The impact of that has been that all of the money that was in the tally-averaging fund of some $70 million has been used up so now western farmers are facing a $100 million increase in the cost of the transportation of grain. The price they will have to pay to transport grain will increase from $6 a tonne to about $9 a tonne at a time when the value of a tonne of grain is dropping from $130 to $105 per tonne, if we believe what the Minister of Agriculture and the Wheat Board Advisory Committee have reported to us. However, we should wait, of course, to hear exactly what the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) will say.
March 5, 1987

We are facing a difficult time. The Minister of Finance increased personal taxation by 50 per cent in the last three Budgets. The Minister of Transport has increased the cost of shipping grain by 50 per cent. The Minister responsible for the Wheat Board has reduced the initial price of grain over the last three years from $170 a tonne to $105 a tonne. The Minister of Agriculture said yesterday at the Canadian Federation of Agriculture meeting that in fact farmers should not count on massive support this year. At a time when the worst financial disaster to strike western Canada is before us, the Minister is telling us not to count on support.
There is one footnote to this difficult time in western Canada and that is the fact that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) is carrying out a wide-scale tax audit of farmers' investment tax credits in Manitoba and Saskatchewan particularly. The farmers claimed these tax credits in 1983 and 1984. If there is anything unnerving to farmers it is to see that kind of widespread tax audit going on. I believe that many farmers who are being audited are honest, responsible people who have bought machinery, tractors or combines after entering into legitimate, fair and proper contracts. Now the Department of National Revenue is sending its men throughout the country at a time when farmers are under extreme financial stress. The Department of National Revenue is moving across the Prairies calling into question these accounts.
Yesterday I had a meeting with a number of producers from the Canadian Cattlemen's Association. A producer from near Saskatoon described the initiative on the part of the Department of National Revenue as being a whole can of worms. He made a fair deal to purchase a combine. I have forgotten the exact figures, but the same techniques are always used. The farmer buys a combine or a tractor at, say, $100,000. He pays $40,000 or $50,000 to the farm implement company and then signs the agreement and pays the money or makes arrangements to borrow the money to make the payments. Now, three or four years later, the tax department embarks on a program which the Government is, incidentally, phasing out, and this is also causing a great deal of hardship. Officials from the Department of National Revenue are saying that the amounts allowed on tractors or combines are not right. The farmer was not terribly concerned about how much he was allowed for his tractor or combine. He was concerned about the difference. However, the dealer sold the machine at list price, and now the tax department is changing the rules. The producers I talked to yesterday are going to court to fight it all the way. We hear that repeatedly from farm communities, particularly those in Manitoba and Saskatchewan. They say they get great sympathy from the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board, but not from the Minister of National Revenue. When we put questions to him in the House, he said this is a general program. That may be, but it is farmers who are being nailed. We think what the Government is doing is extremely unfair and it should be called off.
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
I do not want to hold up passage of this Bill. It should have been passed last October, and I suppose its main impact will not be felt until next September or October. However, the advantages will be felt at that time, and it is a beneficial package. I hope the Minister will soon make a statement concerning the initial price of wheat, the assistance to be provided in the way of a deficiency payment, and on what basis, so that farmers will know whether it is possible to plant a crop this year. It is important that the Government clarify these points quickly so producers will know where they are in the coming year.

Mr. Speaker, I want to begin with a comment on the comment by the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer). On October 21, when the Minister first spoke on this Bill, I suggested that it could be referred to committee at the end of that sitting. Many of the factors which led to the crisis in Canadian agriculture are still in place. That is what I said then, but it was not referred to committee at that time. I now want to go to part of the reason why I suggested that it go through. I quote directly from page 588 of Hansard of October 21, 1986, where the Minister said:
I hope the Opposition will look at this legislation very favourably and give it reasonably quick passage. There are a couple of provisions which, if we can pass this Bill without a lot of delay, can actually be of some use to producers this year. Most of the amendments will have to wait until next year before they will have full effect, but some amendments, if we can have reasonably quick passage of the Bill, will be of use to producers this year.
That is a direct quote from the Minister from last October 21. We believe everything the Minister says, so we thought they could be used last year.
I will not spend too much time on the Bill because we have already spoken on it. We support it at third reading. We got it through committee in one sitting and back into the House by December 3, which was much later than we had hoped or expected. It has not come back before the House until now.
Grain used to move through the system only at the call of the exporters. Back in the old days this meant a great variation in the prices paid for grain when the farmer brought it to the elevator. At that time the location of the farmer could be a great advantage. Farmers who lived near Winnipeg could get into the market earlier. Those who lived in the Peace River country or in northern Saskatchewan, as I do, had problems getting the crop in when it was needed. Those farmers could
The quota system solved this problem to some extent, but did not solve the problem of not being able to deliver on time. Farmers still needed the money as soon as harvest was over, and they could not earn it as effectively as they may have under other circumstances. There are still some problems with it. For instance, last year there was no quota until the end of October, which meant that farmers did not receive any cash flow until that time. The situation still exists to a certain degree today.
The answer to this broad problem was the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act which was introduced by the Member for Qu Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) when he was the Minister. In introducing that Act he attempted to solve both of those problems at the same time and, effectively, succeeded. That was not only an advantage to the farmers, but also an advantage to the Wheat Board because there was not so much pressure on it to ensure that every farmer had an opportunity to deliver some grain. If their particular type of grain was not called for, the farmers could get an advance payment instead and did not have that much of a problem. This allowed the Wheat Board to be much more specific in calling the type of grain it needed for the sales it had made. Now, five or six weeks before the boat to be loaded arrives at the harbour, the Wheat Board calls up enough grain to fill the boat without any time being lost.
This Bill amends a very important part of the cash flow structure of farmers. It is, to some extent, a housekeeping Bill in that it straightens out problems that have shown up over the years in the advance payment structure. With regard to productivity, farmers who are producing far above the average per acre will be able to use the grain they have on hand rather than the amounts of grain which would be expected to be produced on those acres. That is very important in northern Saskatchewan, northern Alberta and northern Manitoba where we produce much larger crops per acre than they do in the south. As the Minister suggested, the yield of farmers who are irrigating is doubled again. That, therefore, is a worthwhile change.
The provision for current interest rates is a relief needed badly by some farmers who are in default. It is very bad that they are being charged higher levels of interest. Under this Bill the landlord is no longer required to sign. A real problem for a farmer-producer who was renting from five different people was that he had to get five different signatures before he could get an advance payment, even if the advance was on grain which had nothing to do with the landlords. This Bill gives the Minister the power to have forms passed without going before the Cabinet, which makes good sense. The provision for emergency advance payments for unthreshed grain and drying without going before Cabinet is a logical approach because it is the Minister who will make that recommendation to Cabinet in the end. Finally, the fact that grade will be recognized in the amount of the advance payment means that a farmer can get
March 5, 1987

more advance payment for less grain if he has higher quality wheat or, vice versa, he can use a larger portion of his wheat at a lower level.
The suggestion made by the Hon. Member for McKenzie (Mr. Scowen) that the Minister should have the authority to make advance payments at the start of the crop year to enable producers of grain to better finance the drying of damp and tough grain has some value, particularly in my part of the country. I believe we could have much more higher quality grain coming off the fields if farmers were willing to take it off a little earlier and dry it. Last year is a good example. The division between No. 3 and No. 1 was large enough. With no payment on No. 1 and No. 2 it did not make that much difference, but it could have made a large difference. With No.
1 and No. 2 being our prime products, it is important that we encourage farmers to produce as much of the high quality grains as possible because they are the grains which many of the buyers are looking for.
We will push this legislation through as quickly as we can today. However, I want to take this opportunity to comment on a couple of other things relative to farming. This particular Bill is one of a series, I suppose, of Bills which have been passed over the years to allow farmers to have some kind of security that at the end of the year the production from their land will bring them enough at least to pay the cost of preparing the land, planting and harvesting. They should have some feeling of security that there is going to be a return for their work and investment. The legislation we now have in place has given considerable support to the farmers, that is, the Western Grain Stabilization Act, the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act and the deficiency payments brought in last year.
These are all factors which contribute to some kind of security for a farmer that when he plants in the spring he will at least be able to pay his costs in the fall. However, that kind of security is fast disappearing. It disappeared to some extent last year, and this year it is of major concern to farmers. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and, I suppose, the Cabinet in general, need to look at farming in general. They need to take a global look or, I suppose a better word would be a "national" look at agriculture, and try to put in place something which would ensure, within certain conditions and reasonable limits, that a producer who produces well and is efficient will at least get back his cost of production.
After the last year of disaster, to some extent, in grain prices, we now have a situation where farmers are finding they really do not know what they should seed next year. They do not even know if they should seed at all. If they do not receive some commitment or some security of return, we cannot be surprised if many farmers decide they just cannot afford the fertilizer and therefore will not put it in. Many of them might say they cannot afford the spray so they will not use it, or they may decide they cannot even afford to summer fallow this year
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
because the cash flow is too small. Those are the kinds of questions producers in the Prairies are asking themselves and the kind of questions we here in this House must be able to address. We should be able to give them some answers which would make them a little more secure than they are at the moment.
There may be no seeding this year, unless we have some kind of commitment from the Government that there will be a return at least at the level of last year, and there are other areas in which the Government could take action.
It is very interesting that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in speaking to a group of people yesterday suggested that he could do nothing about the problems of the Prairies, that they were world problems. The problems of the farmer are spread between the cost of production and what he receives for his product. Therefore, there are two things which can be done. Either we can guarantee a higher level of return or we can do something about the cost of production. There is no reason why the Government could not look at a rebate for farmers of taxes on fuel. There are a lot of costs relative to the use of fertilizer such as the taxes on gas to be used in the fertilizer machinery. There are the taxes on fertilizer, generally. The cost of fertilizer could be reduced. Even the cost of chemicals could be reduced by allowing generic chemicals, which the Government is moving towards to some extent, and by making sure it does not take its pound of flesh each time a product for farming is purchased by the farmer.
At the moment the greatest factor in costs of production to farmers is the interest which is paid for their debt. The Government could put a moratorium on interest payments for a period of time as long as it does not increase the farmers' debt at the end of that period of time. That would at least give him a cash flow. The farmers at present have no commitment to ensure that they will receive the cost of their seed back if they plant this spring. They need that assurance, otherwise we are going to have a tremendous number of farmers making a decision-which they may in the end make anyway-to get out of farming. They are going to start making that decision before their spring work this year because they really have no incentive for starting that cycle of production.
I think it is important that Hon. Members of this House recognize the problems faced by the grain farmers. I could spend a lot of time on that subject. I hope members of the Government who are farmers are making the point as often as possible with their colleagues in Cabinet that low prices are the cause but increasing the prices is not the only solution. We can do it in other ways. What we need over the next couple of years is a structure which will allow the survival of the farmers who are now on the land. We have had about six years of culling out those farmers who are inefficient and bad managers. This has been going on for six years. Why should it continue? Most of the people who are presently farming are efficient farmers and producers. The concern I have is that they be given the opportunity to survive. We in this Parliament

Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
have a responsibility to ensure that it is possible for them to survive.
I am glad the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) is here because there is another area which greatly affects farmers, and that is, transportation itself. It is one of the areas which for many years was the only factor in the farmers' input costs which they could be assured was going to be the same the following year. That was finished a few years ago when the Crow rate was dismantled. We now have greater transportation costs than we had in the past. That is something about which the Government could do something. It would increase the amount of money going back into the pockets of farmers from grains.
It has come to light recently that there are a number of lines in the North which need upgrading. I consider this to be a very unsavoury situation. For instance, in my constituency, the Blaine Lake Subdivision which was supposed to have heavy steel, has been taken off the priority list of the technical committee for some reason which no one can put their finger on. I suggest it is probably because of political interference.
These types of situations do not help farmers. They create the type of environment in which they feel that everything is going against them. What the Government and all of us should be doing is putting in place the type of structure that would give them the security to go on producing.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to stand today in my place and talk about Bill C-12 and other matters which I would like to bring to the attention of the House. I commend the Minister for his excellent coverage of the Bill. I think that because he has covered it so well we do not have to talk too much about it. I understand that Members of the House are in agreement with this particular Bill. I think it has been agreed that we should pass it as soon as possible.
I would like to make a few comments on what the Minister stated about my proposal with respect to the drying of grains in certain areas which, over the years, have suffered from heavy rainfalls. A lot of people do not understand this situation, which is why I would like to explain it. The Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) and I come from a part of the country which is along the fringe of a forest area. To the north there are a great many lakes and trees which attract rainfall. We have a higher amount of rain than the rest of the province, which allows for increased production in most years as compared to the other prairie provinces. This is all fine and dandy when the crop is growing. However, when harvest time rolls around it becomes a public nuisance, which makes it very difficult to harvest the grain when it is in its peak period.
March 5, 1987
The Bill in front of us calls for the Minister to be given a chance to give a cash advance in case of emergency. In our particular part of the country the emergency starts at the time the crop is ripe. As the rains fall on the crop, the quality of the grain quickly deteriorates. Not only does the grain drop in quality but the number of bushels for which the farmer is finally paid decreases. For instance, we now try to swath our grains, and wheat in particular, about the third week in August. Of course, the seeding time usually establishes when one's crop is ripe. We try to let it ripen to a certain standard. We swath the grain and try to pick it up within about four days, depending on the weather, and then we dry it.
Over the last few years we have been successful in producing No. 1 and No. 2 wheat in the particular area about which I am talking. These grains weigh up to about 65 pounds per bushel and are of high quality. Those who are not fortunate to get their crops off early, having to leave it until October, will have grain that will weigh as little as 55 pounds per bushel. It usually turns out to be No. 3 grain or feed grain, which causes a considerable loss to farmers, both in terms of bushels and in price.
I have always been an advocate of trying to get the crop off and drying it. Our farmers have had dryers for many, many years. Even though one may have a dryer it is not always possible to follow the process. However, with dryers and modern combines we can harvest the grain. The straw is tough and the grain may be fairly tough. With modern dryers we can usually salvage a fairly good grain. This is the reason I would like to try this particular run along the fringe line in our area.
I think the Canadian Wheat Board keeps pretty good records with respect to what is dried and what is not. It can tell from the samples it takes. I think this would be a beneficial experiment. If it were it could expand into other areas. Over the last couple of years the Prairies have suffered from deterioration of crop. Farmers on the Prairies have not had the experience of drying grain as we have had in the North. They have had a few disasters. For example, they have burned grain and so on and so forth simply because they do not know how to operate the dryer in an emergency. They try to do things too quickly. We use the same type of equipment but because of our experience with this problem we are able to dry the grain very nicely.
Something I did not mention earlier is the fact that in the early part of the year when the humidity is down and the temperature is up the cost of drying grain in late August to early September is about two-thirds less than when it is done in October or November when the humidity is higher and the days are shorter. At that time of year temperatures are considerably lower. Even the temperature of grain is down to the point where the cost of just bringing its temperature up to where the moisture can be brought out of it is considerable.
I would now like to make a couple of comments with respect to the speech of the two previous speakers. The Hon. Member for Prince Albert made some very good suggestions. I have to agree with his observations with respect to what is going on at
March 5, 1987

the present time. There are a great many problems out there. I think that we should get together on some of the problems in order to make life a lot easier for our farmers. They are now in a position in which it is difficult to have optimism with respect to what to do. As Members of Parliament I think we have to work together to try to get a number of these problems solved. This Bill is one of the ways in which we are trying to do this. The Special Canadian Grains Program was another one. Between the Special Canadian Grains Program and the Grain Stabilization Program, farmers should be able to receive enough money by seeding time to put in a crop. We also must get together and solve the further problem of the shortfall in income of the farmer for another year. I have some suggestions on that problem.
I wish to comment on the points raised by the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster). I agree with him on some points, and there are some that I object to. I take the signal from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) a little differently from him in what he has said about what the Government may or may not do in the future.
The signal that I receive from the Minister of Agriculture is that farmers should be careful not to overdo the planting of crops this year and should try to stay within a reasonable amount of planting simply because there may not be a great amount of money to cover twice as much crop as there was this past year. That creates a problem with an over-production situation. We must be careful when telling farmers what we are doing to encourage production. I do not agree with the Hon. Member for Algoma when he stated that we are very low in the polls, and there are a lot of problems there for our side.
You may not bottom out yet.

That is quite possible, we may not bottom out
yet.
In my experience, and I have a few years on the Hon. Member and probably a little more experience, the most popular boss does not always do the best job. In my experience, whether it is a boss or whether it is a president of a club, the one who is not the popular one is usually the one who gets the job done. Our farmers want the job done and our economy back in place. When the smoke clears, we will find that all is well in the Canadian economy with the way things are being done at the present moment. I have to bring that touchy subject up.
Another subject that I would like to talk about is one that I have brought to the attention of the House many times, that is, the interest rate set by the Farm Credit Corporation and the situation that was created in 1982 by the previous Government. I realize that the Act that was introduced in 1982 can be amended. I think that it should be amended so that the Farm Credit Corporation conforms with the original intent of that program. It was there to assist farmers, not to charge them an interest rate that they cannot possibly pay. Farmers cannot
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
pay that interest rate at this particular time. They cannot pay penalties on land that they are trying to sell to cut down their capital cost and interest. The farmers cannot handle the situation that presently exists in the Farm Credit Corporation.
I would like to see the Farm Credit Corporation set up a different system and establish a separate corporation where farmers and the Farm Credit Corporation, or farmers and banks, would be able to go to a separate corporation and put their joint equity into one place. This would allow the banks to maintain the holding price on their books at a level that would allow the farmer to have an equity in the joint venture. The farmer would be allowed to buy back his shares so that eventually he would own the land. I have approached the Farm Credit Corporation on this subject, and I would like to bring the Farm Credit Corporation back in front of the Standing Committee on Agriculture to try to find a way to set up this idea.

I was interested in the comments of the Hon. Member for Mackenzie (Mr. Scowen). He has put forward some important items with regard to the Bill before us, and the impact it will have on his area.

It is his Government which also cut the federal share of funding for health and post-secondary education by $2 billion, and now it wants to cut get federal-provincial co-operation to fund research.
Can the Prime Minister now say how the deficit ridden poorer provinces will participate in his program when their equalization grants are also being cut back?
I call on the Prime Minister to say if and when his research policy will get Canada closer to the accepted expenditure target of 2.5 per cent of the Gross National Product. Scientific and university communities in Canada are waiting for these answers, not more speeches that make more vague promises about our scientific future.

subtopic: SIGNING OF CANADA-CHINA FILM CO-PRODUCTION AGREEMENT
SIGNING OF CANADA-CHINA FILM CO-PRODUCTION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know all Members of the House will join with me in recognizing the work of the Hon. Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) on her trip to the People's Republic of China. The Minister has succeeded in signing a film coproduction agreement with China as part of her visit to promote Canadian culture and telecommunications.
A co-production agreement is a legal accord between two governments intended to lessen the cost and risk of film production. This agreement allows film producers to draw on Government, business and private funds in both countries. Under the agreement, films are made as co-productions and are considered to be national films in both participating nations. The agreement can also ease restrictions on the movement of people and equipment across borders to facilitate production.
In the past Canada has signed film co-production agreements with France, Italy, Germany, Israel, and the U.K. This agreement is a major achievement for Canada and is the first co-production of this magnitude ever undertaken by China. The Minister's and the Government's commitment to international film production should be applauded.

In view of the fact that an Israeli inquiry found that Yaron was well aware that more than 700 Palestinian civilians were brutally murdered by Christian militiamen in the Sabra and Shatila camps in Lebanon, this action is entirely appropriate. We know well the history of that slaughter in September of 1982, and the action taken by the Minister in placing Canada's position clearly on the record in this area is to be commended. Finally, I would note that this was done despite the fact that General Yaron was accredited to Washington. The Minister must be congratulated.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity today to speak on Bill C-12 as presented in the House of Commons. The Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) made some very eloquent remarks earlier today and described for us the Bill and its details. I will try to touch on some issues which concern me and which I believe concern much of the agricultural community across the country as they pertain to this piece of legislation and about farming issues generally.
First, we know that the cash advance is based on grain stored and not necessarily on acreage. We know that the interest rate on defaulted advances is a floating rate instead of a fixed rate as it had been in the past. Of course, generally that is a good thing because it will assist in bringing the rate down for some people who are financed at a higher rate. However, we are hoping that the Government would bear in mind that in the unfortunate possibility that interest rates rise again, there should be some way of assuring the farming community that the floating rate will not become a floating rate similar to that of chartered banks which in the past brought those rates up very dramatically because interest rates had risen. I do have a concern about the potential for the future. Of course, in the immediate future it will be of benefit to those people who will be able to reduce their payments.
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
As I understand it, the total of the cash advance will be $30,000 and those people applying under this Bill will not be able to apply as well under the advance payment Act. Of course, this could lead to abuse as, I understand, it has on occasion in the past. I also understand that there is an escape clause for farmers who cannot deliver grain under certain special circumstances.
All of this will, of course, be a modest improvement. We should remember, however, that the main issue is not being addressed. I know that it is not the specific purpose of this Bill, the Bill to the amend the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, to resolve all the problems of grain producers. No one pretends that that is the role of this Bill. However, it should be noted nevertheless that it is high time the Government became aware of the major concerns of the agricultural community and saw to it that some of these issues are resolved.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Algoma, raised in the House previously the possibility that the price of wheat will go down from somewhere in the order of $3 to $2.50 this year in terms of payments made by the Wheat Board. I must say that that is a very big concern for Canadian farmers. Over the last few days, we have heard of the concern and worry that exists in the community. People are wondering if it is worth their while to seed this year. That is a very unfortunate kind of decision that farmers will be faced with making this year. As unfortunate as it is, I think we should realize that it is not something that will be necessary for only one year. Unfortunately, there are many more years during which the U.S. Farm Bill will apply, and therefore the problems in the agricultural community will be there for some time. It could be that unless the Government faces reality, that very unfortunate decision some farmers may have to make in the next few weeks will apply not just for one year but for several years to come or at least until the expiry of the U.S. Farm Bill.

Last year, Mr. Speaker, together with some of my colleagues, I had the opportunity to visit Washington. On that occasion, we were briefed about the American farming legislation. I can assure you that the message we got from the United States was very dismal indeed for all Canadian farmers.

The U.S. Farm Bill or the United States Food Security Act, 1985, is one of the reasons there are all these problems in the agricultural community at this time. Perhaps the United States is not the only cause of this problem. There are a number of other causes for the difficulties in the agricultural community now, including the fact that the United States enacted the United States Food Security Act, 1985, as a retaliatory measure against the European Economic Community which was, in the eyes of the United States, subsidizing its own agriculture to a level which was unfair. It was basically these unfair subsidies from the EEC that apparently caused

the United States to impose its own unfair subsidies to match the other ones.
Of course, the Canadian farmer is not faced with the possibility of competing against the U.S. farmer or the European farmer but in fact is competing against the Treasuries of the countries of western Europe and the United States put together. Canadian farmers are very effective and productive. Some would say that they are too productive since there is an over-abundance of product at the present time. It is unusual, though, that those very productive Canadian farmers are having such difficulty making ends meet. They certainly do not deserve to face the hard time they are facing now. However, because they are competing against the subsidies of foreign countries, they are nevertheless faced with this very difficult situation.
When my colleagues and I visited Washington last year, we attended a briefing session at which we asked representatives of the Canadian Embassy in Washington what efforts had been made by the Government of Canada to attempt to have this particular Bill either delayed, changed or altered in such a way that it would not damage Canadian agriculture as it has now. We asked our representatives in Washington specifically which lobbying firm they had hired in order to fight off this very offensive piece of legislation. Of course, we know that in the past, Canada has hired United States lobbyists. Mr. Deaver is one example of a lobbyist who was hired to lobby on the issue of acid rain. There was quite a bit of controversy over that, but we will not touch on that at this time. The point is that for other very important issues, the Government of Canada sought the assistance of professionals in order to ensure that we had as much help as possible to either delay, defeat or alter legislation before the U.S. Congress.
When we asked our people in Washington what kind of resources they had to fight off the U.S. Farm Bill, a Bill containing $70 billion in U.S. subsidies, they said that they did not hire anyone. Of course, that is not the fault of the staff of the embassy, that was a decision that should have been made by the Government of Canada. The staff of the embassy were,
I am sure, doing their best with their own limited resources. There were one or two people with expertise in agriculture lobbying 535 U.S. legislators.
Not surprisingly, the United States adopted the U.S. Farm Bill. It did not change it in any way to accommodate Canada. It did not alter it in such a way that it could provide any form of relief for us. Following the passage of the U.S. Farm Bill, First Bank Agri-Services, which I gather is a division of the Bank of Montreal, commissioned a study to be done by Chase Econometrics Incorporated. Chase Econometrics, a very reputable firm, undertook the study which predicted the effects the U.S. Farm Bill would have on Canadian agriculture. Looking at some of the tables in this document, you will see the basic loan rates for major U.S. crops over the next two years. The basic loan rate is for all intents and purposes nothing less than the price you get for your product. In 1985 the U.S. price for wheat was $3.30, and $2.55 for corn. They
predicted it would be $2.40 to $2.70 in 1986, $2.28 to $2.85 in 1987, $2.17 to $2.71 in 1988, $2.06 to $2.57 in 1989, and $1.95 to $2.44 in 1990. According to that study, the price of agricultural commodities will go down every single year from now until the end of 1990.
It is very sad to have to make public that kind of information. It tells me that the Government of Canada will have to develop a very serious aid program for the agricultural community, not just for the next three or six months but from now until the end of 1990. That is when the U.S. Farm Bill expires. It is not you or I who will be able to convince the Americans, now that they have passed this unfortunate legislation, to alter it. It is too late. We should have done our work properly before the Bill was passed. We should have lobbied, we should have sent delegations, including Members from both sides of the House. We should have employed the Canada-U.S. parliamentary group. We should have done everything to try to make our American counterparts aware of the fact that we, their trading partner and ally, were going to be very seriously affected by this legislation. But we did not do anything.
It is unfortunate that the Government of Canada did not see fit to do whatever was in its power in order to obtain amendments or, even better, defeat that legislation.
The challenge now is for the Government of Canada and, yes, its taxpayers to support the agricultural community during this time of crisis. The crisis will not end after a few months. The Bill was passed in December of 1985, signed by the President, and it will be there until 1990.
I will just take a few moments to describe some of the features of that legislation just in case the people in the grain industry think they are the only ones suffering. They are not, but of course that will not make them feel much better because their difficulties will remain. By the time that U.S. legislation has expired there are several other areas of agriculture that will have been hurt. Section 104 of the legislation deals with the avoidance of an adverse effect of the milk production and termination program on beef, pork and lamb producers. According to Canadian government officials, this could depress international prices and North American domestic prices and displace Canadian exports to Third World countries. Section 153 will depress international prices and displace Canadian exports in the dairy industry. Section 1006 affects wheat and feed grain exports, which is what we are dealing with now. That section provides the Secretary of Agriculture with discretionary authority to establish a program applicable to any of the 1986 to 1990 crops for wheat or feed grain and provide incentives for the export of such crops from private stocks. You no doubt recall the issue being raised in this House about the effect this measure was having on the Canadian agricultural industry. The U.S. was giving extra subsidies for exports and it caused us to lose that export potential or lose customers we already had. There were certain Middle East
March 5, 1987

countries where that has happened over the last few months or so.
[Translation)
Finally, Mr. Speaker, needless to say that I have found in my document pages upon pages of sections in this US Farm Bill which have or could have highly detrimental effects on our agricultural industry.
When the United States is willing to spend 70 billion dollars of their own currency to pre-empt foreign markets and recover their so called fair share of the market-place, the message I get is that a foreign country as a means of retaliation is trying to steal away customers from other nations. I find this quite regrettable.
Even if we support Bill C-12, I should not like my honourable colleagues in the House to return to their ridings over the weekend to make their constituents believe that they have done a lot of good and solved all the problems facing the farming industry, for such is not the case. The problems of the farming community will be with us for quite some time and in the coming years they will certainly require on the part of the House and on the part of the Government and the Canadian public the desire and the collective will to give badly needed support to our farming community.
