speechtext:
I thank the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) for his kind indulgence. It is very appropriate that we are debating this particular Bill today because in the business section of The Globe and Mail this morning there was an article entitled: "Canada a second-rate power moving toward third-rate status, survey says". That particular article was referring to a survey of some 200 leaders from business, government, labour, universities, consumers and women's groups who, according to the report, took part in a poll by Hay Management Consultants and indicated that they believed that Canada is now a second-rate economic power moving toward third-rate status because there are a number of difficult issues confronting Canadians which neither Canadians nor the Government are prepared to face up to. Two of those issues were Canada's declining competitiveness and the excessive regulation of many industries. It therefore seems quite appropriate to me that we are dealing this afternoon with Bill C-21 which deals with both those areas. It is an attempt to provide for greater competition in the liner conference shipping segment of our economy. It is, at the same time, an attempt to try to deregulate that sector to a degree in order to provide for that competition.
This Bill is designed to provide greater competition in liner conference shipping. While it does exempt conferences from certain provisions of the Competition Act, it has three provisions which will encourage greater competition: independent action, confidential service contracts, and a complaint procedure.
Clause 4(3) of Bill C-21 requires shipping conferences, as a condition of exemption from the Competition Act, to provide in their basic agreement the right of independent action for individual members of the conference. Independent action means that a member line can provide a service in a manner or at a rate that is different from those rates provided in the tariff of rates established by the conference. It also includes the provision of a service by a member line that is not provided for in the conference tariff. This provision will allow individual conference members to compete vigorously with non-conference competitors. It provides a means for conference members

March 5, 1987
Shipping Conferences Exemption Act, 1986
to avoid the ponderous, time-consuming rate review committees that conferences have created to review their tariff of rate structure in the past.
A second feature of independent action is a provision that requires a member contemplating independent action to give notice of its intended action to other members of the conference. The benefits of this provision are two-fold. First, it protects the interests of other members of the conference and, second, it encourages other members of the conference to join this rate, thus providing cheaper shipping services to more Canadians. A clause in this section allows other members of the conference to join the independent action on or immediately after the day on which the independent action is first taken. The notice period is important and must balance the need to protect the interest of members of the conference and the need to respond quickly to requests for project rates or other requirements with short response times.
In the past, shippers have criticized conferences for not responding quickly enough to requests for lower rates which are required when quoting prices for particular projects. Shippers, when quoting prices for such projects, must make decisions on the costs in days or weeks and, as transportation is often the most significant element in the over-all cost, they need a decision on a reduced rate within the same time frame. Too often a representative of a conference member line undertakes to get a lower project rate established by the conference only to return in two or three weeks to indicate that, although the line he represents was prepared to carry the goods at the proposed rate, the other members of the conference turned down the request. In addition, to ensure that shippers are aware of this competitive rate, the conference must publish the independent action rate or service item not later than ten days after the receipt of the notice.
The independent action provision will encourage conferences to be more responsive. Canadian exporters and importers do not wish to lose contracts and members of the conferences do not wish to lose cargoes for transportation. This provision provides a mechanism whereby individual conference members can provide the response that shippers require and ensure that both shippers and conference members benefit.
Independent action is not a new thing. It has been practised by conferences on a voluntary basis for many years. The difference intended here is that the conference can no longer agree that its members should not take independent action. For some specific commodities conferences may have no rates quoted in their tariff. These rates are commonly called "open rates'. For commodities with open rates individual conference members may, of course, quote whatever rate they wish. This is a form of voluntary independent action, the sort of thing which this Bill will enshrine.
It is not likely that a large number of independent action rates will appear as a result of this provision. As the action rests with conference members, it is expected that they will agree upon a lower rate in most cases and that the new rate will become the conference rate. This provision will strengthen,
however, the bargaining position of the conference member seeking a lower rate and provide a downward pressure on freight rates, providing benefits to all Canadian importers and exporters.
The provisions governing service contracts also provide further elements of competition. Service contracts are defined as a contract between a shipper of goods and one or more members of a conference whereby the shipper agrees to provide to those members, for transportation by them over a fixed period of time, a specified minimum quantity of goods, and in return those members agree to carry the goods at a specific rate schedule and agree to provide a specific level of service.
The existing act requires all rates to be filed and available for all shippers. This provision has prevented shippers from taking full advantage of their economic power, as conferences must always consider the implications for their total trade. Clause 4(I)(c) of Bill C-21 allows conferences to establish the terms and conditions respecting the use of service contracts by their members. Clause 12 of the Bill ensures that service contracts will remain confidential. The Bill also provides that members of a conference are no longer bound by these terms and conditions after notice is given to the other members of the conference. The conference may establish the length of this notice period but such notice may not exceed 15 days.
A further element of competition can be found in Clause 14(1) of the Bill which deals with the complaint procedure. The existing act requires the Canadian Transport Commission, after receiving a complaint against an agreement or action of a conference, to use the public interest test as the means of determining the suitability of the agreement or act. Bill C-21, on the other hand, allows the Canadian Transport Commission to order the conference to remove the offending feature of an agreement or action if that feature has, or is likely to have, by a reduction in competition, the effect of producing an unreasonable reduction in transportation service or an unreasonable increase in transportation costs.
All of these elements of Bill C-21 combine to provide a significant increase in competition in the liner conference shipping area while ensuring that the public interest is protected. That is, of course, exactly what the article in The Globe and Mail today referred to, the survey by the Hay Consulting Firm which indicated that Canada was slipping as an economic and trading nation because of our declining competitiveness and excessive regulations of many industries. This Bill is aimed at correcting, at least in part, those problems, and I trust Hon. Members of the House will agree to pass it quickly in order to ensure that Canada retains a first rate position in the world of trading nations once again.

subtopic: SHIPPING CONFERENCES EXEMPTION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to take part in the second reading debate of Bill C-21, to repeal the Shipping Conferences Exemption Act, 1979, and
March 5, 1987

to exempt certain shipping conference practices from the provisions of the Competition Act.
I must say that, as former Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, it is difficult for me, as a matter of principle, to accept a bill which provides exemptions from the Competition Act. However, I know that shipping operations must take into account what is going on throughout the world, and there have been similar pieces of legislation in Canada throughout the years. However that may be, I am still very reluctant to accept such a bill which exempts an important sector of the Canadian economy from the provisions of the Competition Act.
Second, I must also say that I am very reluctant to accept this Bill because it follows from the general principles contained in the policy statement of the Conservative Government entitled Freedom to Move. This Bill, along with Bills C-18 and C-19, which were recently debated in this House, represents the entire policy of this Conservative Government and reflects an overly favourable leaning toward large Canadian shippers. I repeat that the biggest Canadian shippers are clearly favoured by Government policies. I would have no objection if the other shippers also benefited. However, it seems to me that, in all its initiatives, this Government always favours only the wealthiest, the strongest, and the biggest in our society. I find it difficult to explain such a behaviour, such an instinctive reflex on the part of the Government.

Bill C-18, Bill C-19 and now Bill C-21 are all Bills for big shippers, which means that the Government is trying to make us believe that a big shipper Bill means favourable returns for consumers. The logic at the outset could be simple and appealing. However, I think there are many flaws in this policy and approach of the Government. Unfortunately, these Bills place some big shippers of given goods in a favourable bargaining position vis-a-vis the carriers and vis-a-vis the other small shippers. Theoretically this could lead to lower transportation costs for the shippers and the savings should normally be passed on to the consumer. Unfortunately, it does not always happen that way.

What makes me sad, Mr. Speaker, is that this proposal might at first glance seem attractive, especially for a Government which is systematically and shamefully taxing the middle and lower classes of our society and whose budgetary demagogy has virtually cost it the respect of the entire population-if we ask people whether they are satisfied with their Government, whether they still have confidence in this Government, everyone spontaneously says that they feel wronged and frustrated as this Government thinks only of the wealthy and attacks the neediest members of our society through all its initiatives-at first glance, it therefore seems that this would be a perfect opportunity for the Government to improve its image and say that freer trade and deregulation of transport in Canada will benefit the consumers, but I think the situation is
Shipping Conferences Exemption Act, 1986
actually quite different. The reason unfortunately, is the danger that in the long run, because of pressures that may be exerted by the major Canadian shippers on transportation companies, we will rapidly be faced with a significant number of transportation company bankruptcies or wind-ups in Canada. And those shippers, who originally would have liked to benefit from lower costs and other windfalls brought about by deregulation, will be the first to get caught and forced to surrender to a few large corporations which will control the transportation market and will then set their own rates.
I think the danger in that deregulation exercise is the possibility that the supply of transportation in Canada become too heavily concentrated into the hands of few companies. Whether it be rail transportation or trucking, airlines or even shipping companies, that deregulation exercise can bring about disaster and job losses to thousands of Canadians. Only this week, before the Transport Committee, officials of CP Rail told us that because of this Government's deregulation proposals, some 8,000 miles of rail will have to be abandoned by the CPR because of maintenance costs and because of pressures for lower freight rates stemming from deregulation. Now, 8,000 miles of rail, that means whole communities, towns and villages will be without the service they had grown accustomed to. This means that remote areas in Canada will simply be abandoned because market logic requires that anything not profitable is slashed. And this is what CP Rail will be doing.
We believe that essentially the same thing can happen in the shipping industry if this Conservative legislation is enacted as it now stands. There is a danger that the larger shippers may exert pressure on the conferences, which will obviously bring rates down. This of course will profit a few major shippers, but it can also force out of business the conferences that are now serving the Canadian public.
The ramifications of the Bill are all the more disquieting that, if one reads the briefs that were submitted by the various conferences, there does not appear to be anyone supporting Bill C-21.
1 will quote just one excerpt from a brief that was submitted by the Eastern Canada Caribbean Rate Association.
This is one of the conferences which has submitted representations concerning Bill C-21. After reading many of the briefs I have come to the conclusion that they all seem to oppose the Government's initiatives. Thus I will not read into the record all of the opposing representations, but I will read one as an example of the type of representations that we are now receiving against this initiative of the Government. I quote the brief of ECCRA, which is the acronym for the Eastern Canada Caribbean Rate Agreement, which states:
ECCRA feels that it cannot stand by in silence facing the prospect of Bill C-21 being enacted into legislation by the Parliament of Canada. Should it become law, this Bill would be highly detrimental to the interests of ECCRA and all

March 5, 1987
Shipping Conferences Exemption Act, 1986
other Conferences shipping to and from Canada. ECCRA feels that Bill C-21 would not make good legislation. There are many provisions which would contribute to this. Prohibitions of the right to establish "multi-modal rates", prohibition of 100 per cent loyalty contracts, ambiguity in certain terms such as "predatory practices", "designated shipper group", and "ocean carrier", and yet another sunset clause are all of some concern to ECCRA. However, the most troubling provisions are those concerning Independent Action and Service Contracts contained in Section 4 of Bill C-21.
It is the position of ECCRA that the Conference system in Canada would be destroyed if the new legislation fails to allow Conferences the right to regulate service contracts. This right currently exists under U.S. legislation and prohibiting such Conference control in Canada will create uncertainty and instability within the Canadian shipping industry. ECCRA earnestly believes that Conferences must be able to decide whether service contracts should be entered into with the shippers by the Conferences or by the individual lines. It should be pointed out that such an imbalance between the Canadian legislation and the corresponding U.S. legislation could be very dangerous. The present competition from American ports like New York and Seattle-
There are many other American ports that are not mentioned in this paper which come to mind. I am thinking in particular of the ports of Boston, Portland and others that could be in competition with Canadian ports.
-represent a potential drain of cargo from Canadian ports.
Most other major trading nations such as the U.K., Germany, Japan, Korea, Taiwan and Sweden have little or no legislation regulating Conferences. Conferences have been allowed to operate freely as this has been considered to be in the national interest of those countries. The federal Government of Canada should be doing everything it can to encourage carriers and Conferences to operate in Canada, not to discourage them by increasing regulation, creating uncertainty and perhaps legislating their demise.
Canadian government policy has been to allow and encourage Conferences to operate in Canada. At the same time it has been government policy to encourage and foster healthy competition. These two policies are not contradictory. Conferences certainly do not fear competition and have existed for some time in an environment of fierce competition. Low rates are already the reality of today's market-place. However, Section 4 of Bill C-21 could quite possibly lead to the destruction of the Conference system operating in Canada and gravely damage the national interest. The possible ramifications of the current provisions in Bill C-21 need to to be thoroughly examined and most certainly Section 4 should be amended if government policy continues to be to allow and encourage Conferences in Canada.
If that policy has changed, there has been no proper and in depth study done that would justify such a change in policy. ECCRA hopes that the Committee will heed its warning and examine the entire matter in detail before acting.

Of course, this point of view is that of a conference. I am not ready to endorse entirely this statement before having the chance to question the authorities of the Department who have drawn up this Bill. I do not mean the Minister because once again I am sorry the Minister is not present to introduce his Bill and to answer my questions. However, when the legislative or parliamentary committee does consider the Bill I hope the Minister will make a point of appearing before it and submit himself to our questioning. Anyhow, if he fails to appear, we will do as usual and address our questions to his officials who seem to be more interested than he is in transportation matters.
However, it is obvious that we have to raise questions, get some information and learn whether the Government's policy has changed. We know that every five years, the shipping conferences have been granted exemptions from the Competition Act. The 1979 legislation expired in 1984.
We are now in 1987 and the Conservative Government has not yet found the time to introduce a bill to settle this matter. We are only now tackling the matter which should normally have been settled in 1984.
However, as the conference is asking in its paper: Has the policy changed? Bill C-21 now under consideration is entirely different from the legislation introduced in 1979. If we want to extend the 1979 legislation, there is quite a number of useless clauses in this Bill. But if the Government wants to create the impression that it wants to exempt the fishing conferences from the provisions of the Competition Act while suffocating them and making sure that they are not exempted, I suggest that it should come right out and say so. Why play hide and seek with the conferences? If the Government no longer wants the shipping conferences to be exempted from the provisions of the Competition Act, it should say so frankly and not introduce such a Bill. It should declare: From now on, the forces of competition will apply freely, the market place will be wide open, and any shipper will be able to do business with any shipping conference. As shipping conferences, you will not be allowed any longer by mutual agreement to establish what is called a conference and impose your terms and set your prices. The deal should go to the lowest bidder.
From reading this brief, I get the impression that the Government is not doing exactly what it says it is doing. It is using a Bill to extend the 1979 legislation and do more. Do you know what this reminds me of, Mr. Speaker? Bill C-75. The Government tried to use Clause 4 of that Bill to charge a fee to all ships using the St. Lawrence seaway and the Great Lakes for Canadian Coast Guard services. It was a general legislation which provided for a series of changes which everybody accepted or was ready to accept. On top of that, however, there was this Clause 4, and for the first time the Government could arbitrarily charge fees to all Canadian users. You know what happened. The Liberal opposition, supported in this by all the parties involved in the shipping industry in Canada, fought mercilessly to force the Government to delete clause 4 from Bill C-75.
My Montreal colleague, the Hon. Member for Hochelaga- Maisonneuve (Mr. Desrosiers) is smiling, I see. He knows quite well how detrimental Clause 4 of Bill C-75, had it been maintained, would have been to the Montreal harbour, to the transportation of goods in the Montreal harbour and all the other harbours along the St. Lawrence river. Thanks to the representations of the Montreal Board of Trade, the transport minister of the Quebec government, and a journalist of the Journal de Montreal who wrote a very important report in which he insisted and tried to shake up the Minister of Transport to get him to change this famous section 4, the Government finally came to its senses and recently introduced Bill C-34, which was a true copy of former Bill C-75 of the last session, but without the famous section 4.
I wonder if the same thing might happen with Bill C-21. Taking advantage of the fact that it must renew the agreement under the Act of 1979, the Government comes to us with a bill
March 5, 1987

and says: Now that the five years the legislation was to apply are over, we must give the exemption back to the shipping conferences, and that is what we are doing. When one reads the legislation, one realizes there is more to it than that. It is not only more, but even the opposite of what is intended or what we are told is to be done.
I draw the attention not only of the Government but of the public in general to the strange administrative method which seems to come naturally to the Conservative Party. We are not really sure the Conservatives know where they are going. Every time we read the particulars of a bill they introduce, we find out there is much more in the bill than appears at first glance. So, until we start a clause by clause study of the bill, I hope the transport minister will have an opportunity to review this and let us know exactly what his intentions are.
In conclusion, I would like to quote a comment.
-a comment that has been sent to me by Mr. Ronald B. Gottshall who is Managing Director for the Transpacific Westbound Freight Agreement. He has written the following to all the members of the Transport Committee. This gentleman lives in the United States. In light of the tabling of Bill C-21 he felt that he wished to notify us of the danger of this legislation. I wish to quote what he said:
Legislative measures which undermine the ability of the conference system to do its job in promoting rate stability and equity are contrary to the economic interests of a trading nation.
The United States has stood largely alone in taking legislative steps to weaken the conference system, with consequences that have been devastating for its own merchant marine and which, before long, will be shown to have deleterious consequences for its foreign commerce as a whole. Although changes in the law contained in the present Bill largely follow the U.S. model, there is no objective evidence suggesting that U.S.-type changes undermining a conference system are wise or in the national interest of Canada. The premises of the U.S. legislation were accepted by the U.S. without any basis in objective studies, and early experience with the U.S. legislation strongly suggests that these premises are unsound. We would hope that Canada would not follow such a course.
Here again the Canadian Government has a tendency to copy Americans. Here again we see the Conservative Government trying to do exactly what took place in the U.S., without really looking at it and analysing it to find out whether or not it is in the best interests of Canada. The gentleman I just cited volunteered advice. He told us to be careful, that we were copying the American initiative, and that he was not sure it was a good thing. Indeed, it does not seem to have been in the best interests of Americans.
Therefore I ask the Minister why we are trying to do something which does not seem to be right. Is it because we have a phobia that we must do exactly what the Reagan administration is doing? I find it absolutely repulsive that everything initiated by the Conservative Government is a carbon copy of bad American initiatives, particularly in the
Shipping Conferences Exemption Act, 1986
field of transportation. I think we are embarking upon a very dangerous path.
Deregulation in the United States, as we know, has created many difficulties and many problems. A number of areas in the United States have been deprived of services they used to have as a result of deregulation. Thousands of employees in the transportation field have lost their jobs in the United States because of deregulation. However, we have a Government which blindly follows the American experiment with its Bill C-18, Bill C-19, and Bill C-21.1 hope the Government will wake up before it is too late and will look at it in a way which protects the Canadian interest.
I have no objection to being friendly with the Americans or to believing that the United States of America is a great country. However, that does not mean that we must be a carbon copy of that country. Certainly our Government must consider the Canadian interest first, not necessarily the North American approach to everything which comes under discussion between Canada and the U.S.
American authorities have put pressure upon the Conservative Government to deregulate the transportation field. We know why. If we deregulate the transportation industry in Canada there is a great chance that substantial chunks of our trucking industry will be taken over by the Americans. We have been told that with deregulation and with the implementation of Bill C-18 and Bill C-19, Canadian railways are bound to lose a lot of traffic to American railways. We have been told time and time again that the deregulation process of the current Government would substantially benefit American transportation companies.
It is important that the Government wants to help Canadian shippers. I have no objection to doing our best to help them, but I do not want it to be done in a way which jeopardizes our Canadian transportation industry. If we want to help shippers, let us do it in a balanced way, in a way which takes into account the interests of small shippers as well. I do not want legislation which favours exclusively big shippers through confidential contracts where, because of their power and force, they could negotiate confidential contracts at a much lower rate than they would normally receive.
Who will pay the difference? Obviously small shippers will not receive the same deal on confidential contracts as big shippers. Transportation companies must survive, so what they lose through confidential contracts with big shippers they will get back from small shippers. I do not think the legislation is fair and balanced as it is conceived. Therefore I want reassurance from the various Ministers that Bill C-18, Bill C-19, and Bill C-21 will not impair our vital transportation industry which, over the years, has provided hundreds of thousands of jobs for many Canadians in all parts of the country. In every region of the country there are people working for trucking companies, railways, airlines, and maritime companies. There are good jobs everywhere in Canada in the field of transportation. Unfortunately these jobs are unduly threatened by the action of the Government.

subtopic: SHIPPING CONFERENCES EXEMPTION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Crosbie that Bill C-21, an Act to exempt certain shipping conference practices from the provisions of the Competition Act, to repeal the Shipping Conferences Exemption Act, 1979 and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: SHIPPING CONFERENCES EXEMPTION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to take part in the debate on Bill C-21, an Act to exempt certain shipping conference practices from the provisions of the Competition Act, to repeal the Shipping Conferences Exemption Act, 1979, and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof.
Clearly this Act is one of the package of Bills the Government has put forward to change practices in the transportation industries in and touching on Canada. It is to make changes which are likely to have the most detrimental effect for the companies involved in transportation and to have the most serious effect for those employed in the industry. I regard this
I want to consider some of the problems likely to result from this Shipping Conference Exemption Act, 1986 which is before us. The matter of shipping conferences themselves deserves a little bit of consideration in order to make clear what one is dealing with. Shipping conferences are an organization of carriers involved in a particular direction of trade, an organization to ensure that trade is carried on in an orderly way. What the carriers recognize in coming together in such an organization is that there are possibilities of competitive practices which might be of advantage to someone for the moment, presumably to someone interested in shipping and having some product moved, but which could in fact have a quite serious impact on other carriers in the trade and which would be disruptive to orderly conduct of that trade.
It is obvious in putting it this way that I want to deal in the first part of my comments this afternoon in a fairly penetrating way with competition as it exists in the ocean shipping industry and as part of the recognition of the nature of competition in our economy generally. I think I need to do that because the Government puts forward this Bill with very little regard for its consequences, without an appreciation of the contradictory potential of it. With the Government putting it forward, particularly as a program of removing regulation from transportation, it appears to suggest that completely unregulated, untrammelled, unwatched or supervised competition will somehow be a good thing. If we had competition of that sort in an industry like ocean shipping, Mr. Speaker, we could have predatory pricing practices which would destroy the operations of other competitors in the short run, and which might very well destroy ongoing operations of the company indulging in it. We would have in a competitive situation, if it were completely open, a ship arriving in a port without a cargo, conceivably looking for return cargo, fair game for someone wanting to undercut rates being quoted by others, then grabbing the cargo and going on his way. If the competition were severe between vessels of various carriers, one could see practices of this sort very quickly driving operations into the ground, into a deficit area that would make it impossible for companies to survive.
It was 100 years ago that practices of that sort led to the development of the shipping conferences in the merchant marine of Great Britain. It was the necessity to get some kind of organization of trade to ensure that it would be carried on in an orderly way and in a way that provided an amount of profit to companies which allowed them to pay decent wages to their workers and cover their operations. It was that kind of concern initially that led to the organization of these conferences. The result gradually was the spread of such arrangements from country to country, which has been well described by someone already quoted by the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), Mr. Ronald B. Gottshall, Managing Director of one
March 5, 1987

of the super-conferences these days, the Transpacific Westbound Rate Agreement. Mr. Gottshall has observed in comments on Bill C-21 that:
Every major and successful trading nation permits and in most cases encourages strong conferences in its foreign commerce. Pacific basin and European countries like Japan, Korea, Taiwan, England, Germany and Sweden, whose economies are heavily dependent on exports and imports, all permit a strong conference system. They do so because stability and equity of ocean rate making, which is strong, enforceable conference system provides, promotes the growth of commerce.
Price instability and discrimination in shipping rates, as these successful trading nations have found, is inconsistent with national trading interests and the development of export commerce.
Those observations on the use made by important trading countries of the conference system can be applied to the Canadian situation. We clearly have not obtained all those gains from a sound conference system. One of the results should surely be the development of a Canadian merchant marine operating on the oceans. We have not seen that happen. I regret that very, very much.
We in our Party have long been concerned about the shipbuilding industry across Canada in several great port cities. We have been concerned about the possibilities of developing the steel and other industries that are subsidiary to shipbuilding. We have been concerned about the possibility of employment for Canadians in a merchant marine. We regret very deeply the failure of Governments past, the present Government particularly, but really no less so the Party which is now the Official Opposition and its failure to do anything about the development of a Canadian merchant marine. If we had done that, we would have strength in a variety of productive areas and employment for Canadians.
Perhaps I shall say in all honesty the reason that has not happened is partly the result of international conditions. After the Second World War the United States led the way in encouraging flags of convenience, registry of vessels in Panama, Liberia and other places. Those vessels lacking safety, labour and other provisions were able to undercut any vessels registered in North America. In the United States the domestic shipping industry has been maintained largely because of the Jones Act which has required American bottoms, American registered vessels, for coastal trade. If it were not for that kind of basis, there would not be very much of a registry in the United States either. I realize those were the international factors within which our Governments operated, but I do not think they made any effort to have the system changed in order to encourage a Canadian merchant marine.
Recognizing that the possibilities of a conference system which have been exploited by many countries were not used in the Canadian situation, we now find ourselves faced with the situation of how to regard the conference. My justification for it has been in the way of making possible employment and productivity in Canada, which is only possible if shipping can be carried on in a profitable way by companies registered in Canada. I am clearly putting forward a case for the conference
Shipping conferences Exemption Act, 1986
which is founded on the profitability within checks, of course, of companies involved in ocean shipping.
There, Mr. Speaker, is one of the most ironic aspects of my comments this afternoon and our debate of this Bill. One would expect a Conservative Government to have a due regard for decent profits in every industry, no less so among companies carrying on the business of ocean shipping. I submit that Bill C-21 will be highly disruptive of ocean shipping and will have a most deleterious effect on the profitability of companies in the business now. So many of them are running in the red already in the economic circumstances of our time and Bill C-21 will only make it worse.
I need to say very hastily in making these observations for my caucus that when I talk about the profitability of these companies, I want that to be within a reasonable range of operations. There, of course, is the very basis of our case for regulation. If we are to avoid the cut-throat, destructive competition in ocean shipping which the conference system was designed to prevent, then the only reasonable response to the situation of organization through conference is to ensure that the system is regulated, that the rates are registered with an authority and that there be the possibility of investigations, roll backs and so on. That of course is the system that has prevailed with the Canadian Transport Commission. That is the organization that we want to maintain in this area.
What do we see instead of that? A number of concepts are being put forward by this Bill that will threaten the viability of the conference system which the Bill appears to be renewing and protecting from the competition law of Canada. If it were applied here, it would of course prevent this kind of an agreement or collusion, if you will, among carriers in one particular industry. First, the Bill continues the exemption from the Competition Act, but puts forward mechanisms likely to be quite disruptive to the conference organization for which the Bill allows. It does so by means of two different arrangements. One is the arrangement for independent action and the other is the arrangement for confidential service contracts.
The proposal for independent action is, by its very nature, a destructive feature for the conference. We have an organization of carriers who have established the rules for their trade, including rates that shall be charged, and who ensure that there will be competition in this system on the basis of published rates known to all. At the same time there is a provision for an individual carrier to break with that agreement and establish a rate, which I recognize must be published, allowing it to undercut the arrangement it has made with others.
The length of time that should prevail if independent action were to be allowed is one of the important features here and the Bill in Clause 4 allows a company to take independent action on 10 days' notice. That is not very long. I note from the material Mr. Gottshall presented to us the insistence of one of

March 5, 1987
Shipping conferences Exemption Act, 1986
the conferences, the Transpacific Westbound Freight Agreement organization, that if there is to be independent action, there should be at least 30 days' notice given. Thirty days' notice allows the other members of the conference to react to the situation. It allows them to consider the possibility of matching that rate.
If the point of independent action is to reduce rates, and I am sure those who developed this Bill had that objective, then a competitive process in which the others have time to respond to information that has been given in order to establish a new rate would seem to be a fine result to achieve. Mr. Gottshall also suggests that there should be for these arrangements a life of at least six months to a year, so that this action would be continued and there would be some measure of stability in the industry when such changes take place.
These comments on the matter of independent action are ones that need to be taken very seriously when considering whether or not it is advisable to introduce this disruptive element into the operations of the conference. If independent action is dubious, when we consider the possibility of confidential service contracts, we consider going back to the worst era of companies doing anything to their competitors in order to make money for the short run no matter what may happen in the long run. This particular provision seems to me to be completely incredible. Even if we were to accept the possibility that the Canadian Government is simply aping the U.S. Government in legislation that came into effect two and a half years ago, it would still be completely incredible.
This provision allows a shipper to make a confidential arrangement with one carrier. Surely large shippers who have much cargo to move will have the ability to persuade a particular carrier to reduce the rate for him. He will be allowed under the Bill to keep that rate secret so that others are not sure, although there will undoubtedly be rumours about what kind of contract exists. This arrangement is surely designed to disrupt the conference system entirely. That makes one wonder what is the point of Bill C-21.
If we are to renew the exemption of the conference system from the impact of the competition Act, then why do we have these destructive elements in the Bill? If in fact we do not want the conference system to operate, then let us make it immediately open to prosecution under the Canadian Competition Act and not fool around with a Bill that supposedly extends or renews the exemption while undercutting it in these particular ways.
These proposals for independent action in Clause 4 and for confidential service contracts in Clause 12 are the two most contentious elements in the Bill. There are other smaller items that are not much less contentious than these for those who are involved in the industry. The ironic thing about Bill C-21 is that it is not only the carriers who are opposed to it. There is no doubt that the carriers are opposed to it, as I can assure Hon. Members from what I have seen in the way of briefs presented. The Hon. Member for Papineau has already read substantially from one of those briefs while saying that others
have already come before the Transport Committee. We do have evidence that the carriers are opposed to the Bill, but we also have before us the quite astonishing fact that the Shipping Federation of Canada, an organization of persons in ports who act as agents in the shipping trade, are no less opposed to it. These are the people who have been opposed to the development of the Canadian deep-sea merchant marine, the reason I feel anything but sympathetic toward them. They have come to Members of Parliament with their critique of and opposition to Bill C-21. Regarding the matter of confidential service contracts, they say that these would primarily interest the shippers of commodities, raw materials and semi-finished products, perhaps a dozen such commodities representing a significant percentage of Canada's water-borne exports. They go on to say:
Confidential service contracts would primarily interest the shippers of those commodities and undermine the ability of conferences to be stabilizing forces- so much so that the continued existence of the conference system would be pointless, if not made impossible.
The deep-sea shipping industry has faced a shippers' market for several years now and pressures resulting from the new proposals relating to service contracts and independent action would only lead to lower rates at a time when rates are already at levels which inhibit shipowners from operating profitably. The result of this interaction between shippers and shipowners would not be in anyone's best interests and would result in shippers ultimately suffering a long-term loss for a very minor short-term gain.
We have at times heard about short-term pain for long-term gain. This is promise of long-term loss for a very minor shortterm gain. That is the reaction of the Shipping Federation of Canada to the Bill.
We also have very great concern about what may happen if both Bill C-19, which deals with trucking, and this Bill are passed. The U.S. has so-called private ports, Elizabeth, New Jersey, being one, which have freedom from a good deal of the law on contracting. That results in very low costs. If the trucking legislation is changed in such a way that U.S. trucking companies can run into Canada very easily it becomes quite possible that much of the container business in particular could become centered in a few American ports from which they could be run into Canada. That would have very serious consequences for some Canadian ports, Saint John, New Brunswick, perhaps being the best example. Conceivably Halifax could be affected as well. Who knows what its impact might be in Vancouver. We can see employment in Canadian ports suffering considerably as a direct result of this legislation.
That is an indication of how serious the consequences of this Bill may be and how important it is that the Standing Committee on Transport be allowed to consider it fully. This legislation should go to the standing committee and not be left to a legislative committee to deal with separately. It is part of the deregulation complex and it should be possible for the standing committee to consider the various dangers resulting from this system.
March 5, 1987

The question of what the intention actually is in this legislation forces us to consider for a few moments the context of the American legislation within which the Canadian legislation was surely put forward. The U.S. passed legislation a few years ago in this area and it seems the Canadian Government is putting forward similar or even worse legislation in this Bill. The U.S. does not allow for the confidential service contract. That is a Canadian wrinkle which, as I have said, is likely to be completely disruptive of the industry. Last year, of 29 carriers operating in the westbound trade from North America to Asia, less than half actually belonged to the Transpacific Westbound Rate Agreement. Of those, 13 companies lost an average of $50 million. Among those companies we find U.S. Lines, now undergoing reorganization with a court-appointed receiver because of the financial plight it fell into and in the circumstances which were only made worse by the American legislation. I want to note the following comments of the Shipping Federation of Canada:
Although we are totally opposed, for the above reasons, to suggestions that Canada's legislation emulate that of the U.S., if the Minister is adamant that it be so patterned, then it is our strong recommendation that the passage of new legislation here await the trial period of the U.S. legislation and the study to be conducted by the Federal Maritime Commission as to whether or not it is workable for the longer term. The trial period extends over five years, of which two and a half years have passed, leaving two and a half years more experience to be gained. In the circumstances, it would seem prudent to extend our current legislation until that review has been conducted by the Federal Maritime Commission.
The Federation is well aware of what has happened in the U.S. where it passed a law with little investigation of the situation. Congress legislated in the hope that shipping conferences dominated by other countries in the Pacific, particularly Japanese and Hong Kong interests, would have some sort of freedom of independent action which would allow the American companies to do better against their Asian competitors within the conference system. While the protectionist intent of the legislation was quite clear, its economic effect has been completely destructive of the American companies operating in these conferences. Witness the comments by Ronald B. Gottshall, managing director of the Transpacific Westbound Rate Agreement, speaking in New York on January 8, 1987. In his comments on the policy he says the following:
The last part of the declaration of policy, which states that the Act's purpose is to encourage an economically sound and efficient U.S.-fiag fleet, is one which in my opinion seems doomed to failure as a general purpose of the Act. While there is evidence that there will be an American flag fleet, the question is not "how big?", but instead "how small?".
In my position as managing director of an agreement covering many nationalities and flags, I believe it is essential that each trading partner maintain a presence in trade to represent the transportation interests of its constituents. Without dwelling on the U.S. flag fleet, it's possible that as a result of its adverse effects, the Act won't help anybody.
He then says more specifically concerning the effect of the Act:
Now that we've heard the worst, what do we do about it? Six months ago I was of the opinion that we could survive the five years until review of the Shipping Act and that perhaps even a longer review period was necessary because of the cyclical nature of the shipping business.
Shipping conferences Exemption Act, 1986
Now I'm not sure that we can wait that long. The abuses brought about by "pro-competitive independent action" and "service contracts" have exacerbated the situation, and there may be fatal results for a significant number of carriers before any scheduled review. The shipping public, particularly in the North American trade, customarily presses for faster transit times and more frequent departures; point-to-point services; and systems that will track cargo at any point in the transportation scheme. At the same time, and even though everything they want costs money, many of these shippers firmly believe that transportation costs can be consistently depressed without any effect on the transportation system. To be sure, there was an old saying that, "carriers may go, but ships remain", meaning that there will always be an operator for unemployed vessels.
That truism, of course, depended heavily on the banks who in the past were far more willing to extend operating loans to almost anyone. Today, many banks have backed out entirely or substantially reduced their commitment to the shipping business because of its unpredictability and high default rate. Those banks that are still in the business are less willing to finance new carriers, or even extend credit to existing carriers for expansion purposes where the risk factor is high.
He concludes the speech by saying:
If trade is going to grow and prosper, there must be adequate transportation resources available to carry it. Without being redundant, that takes two things:
A commitment by the carriers to provide the capital and facilities to meet the challenge; and,
A commitment by shippers to pay an equitable price for the services they need and want.
The effect of Bill C-21 will be to allow those shippers who can exploit their strength in the market to force desperate carriers in the short run to undertake contracts that they cannot make a profit on. The result will be quite destructive in the carrier business on the oceans touching on Canada. The fact that 90 per cent of the companies involved in the conferences are owned by Governments of other countries, with the remaining 10 per cent in foreign private hands, if you will, should not be a reason for the Canadian Government to put forward a bill which will be so very, very destructive.

I will conclude my observations on Bill C-21 by pressing, in the strongest possible terms, for this Bill to be considered by the Transport Committee. It is necessary to consider its effects on the ports of Canada, employment in those ports, and on the agencies dealing with the shipping trade in Canada. It is necessary, surely in terms of some regard for the countries, to consider what its effects will be on the various carriers. The fact that the Shipping Federation of Canada is opposed to the Bill, those being the people involved in presenting the cargoes rather than owning the carriers, is the best possible reason to have this matter put before the Transport Committee where it can be properly considered. My colleague, the Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus), and others are very active in this.
The Member for Papineau made some comments on Bill C-75 from the last session. I appreciate that Members can be quite myopic about the rest of the country when celebrating what they accomplished in their own region. However, it is manifestly unfair to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan, and others in my caucus to focus only on Montreal in the battle to have cost recovery for the Coast Guard removed from Bill C-75. The effort was exerted
Shipping conferences Exemption Act, 1986
on the Great Lakes as much as on the St. Lawrence, and perhaps even more, although I do not want to indulge in the same kind of myopic behaviour. The Member for Papineau knows very well as a result of his visit to the Transport Committee, and I believe with the Seaway committee when he came to Thunder Bay last June, that there is as much concern about cost recovery at the head of the Lakes as there is in Montreal. I say that to balance the record on this matter and I am sure he will accept the accuracy of my observations.
I would like to reiterate, underscore, and emphasize in the strongest possible way that Bill C-21 is part of the Government's deregulation package. It will be a destructive element in deep sea transportation as the other Bills will be disruptive in other parts of Canada's transportation industry. We New Democrats think that an industry has the right to make a decent profit. Only with decent profits being made is it possible for workers to negotiate decent wages for themselves while, at the same time, capital obtains the reward that it deserves. In transportation that calls for open, sound organization, information being made available, and regulation of the industry to ensure that the profits do not become excessive. That is our basis for regulation.
I apologize to no one for putting forward this case which respects workers and capital and recognizes the needs of the industry to provide a service as well as recognizing the importance of a well organized transportation industry for all Canadians producers and all those who want the goods. There is nothing for which to apologize. We New Democrats find ourselves in the very strange situation that we are the only ones making such a case these days. The rest of the world seems to have gone mad with some kind of a free enterprise faith and are worshipping very strange gods indeed.
I would like to underscore something which the Hon. Member for Papineau has suggested. There are many briefs before the Transport Committee. The Member read substantially from the brief of the Eastern Canada Caribbean Rate Agreement. I note that the Inter-American Freight Conference has submitted a brief. I have drawn a great deal of advice from the Transpacific Westbound Rate Agreement. The Asian North American Eastbound Rate Agreement has submitted a brief in another direction. I understand that there are 25 briefs expected from the carriers and their organizations. I am sure there will be others.
The Shipping Federation will want to comment on this Bill in a most critical way. They will call for the Government to take it back and give us simply a shipping conference exemption Act and, particularly, to get rid of the provision which exists in the Bill for the confidential service contract. This is not law that the Parliament of Canada should be passing. I call upon the Parliament of Canada to throw it down.

FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS DEFENCE OF QUEBEC'S INTERESTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of establishing a permanent mechanism, consisting of representatives of the government, the official opposition and the government of Quebec, in order to ensure that Quebec interests will be better defended in the future.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think it would be useful to repeat the motion, whose purpose, and I hope it will be supported by all Quebec Members of the House, is to set up a committee representing both Government and Official Opposition Members, as well as the Quebec National Assembly, and thus provide for better defence of Quebec interests that are being neglected here in Ottawa.
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to mention seventeen issues which, after the thirty months this Government has been in power, and that is since yesterday, have yet to be resolved. These are situations where people have lost their jobs and are waiting for the Government to reverse its decision so they can get their jobs back. There are other situations where decisions are still pending, and as a result, jobs and grants will be lost, and also situations where the sick and the elderly are going to have to pay for the federal Government's cutbacks. I would like to mention, one by one, the seventeen Quebec dossiers that are languishing, Mr. Speaker.
First of all, I think everyone will recall the case of Montreal East and Vickers, Bombardier and the plan to attract new businesses under the designated-area program. Nothing has been done yet.
We have the shipyards. We have not only Montreal East but also the Lauzon shipyards near Quebec City, where the Minister, the Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) have been making promises, promises, promises and all kinds of announcements, but nothing has materialized yet and nobody is working in the yards. And we have the same situation in Sorel and Montreal. The only projects people are working on now are the frigate contracts that were awarded under the Liberals.
Mr. Speaker, there is the paper mill in Matane. There is also the Desbiens paper plant in the Lac-Saint-Jean area. During the election campaign, the Prime Minister came on a visit and made promises. The Minister of Employment and Immigration sent a circular letter and held a press conference to announce that the plant would at last be opened. They, the Minister and the Prime Minister, are giving us a lot of talk but no action. The plant is still closed and people are waiting for an answer.
Mr. Speaker, in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean area... and by the way, are there any Member from that area?
Quebec Interests
And what about the potato growers? The Canadian Government decided to pay millions of dollars to potato growers in the Atlantic provinces. There is nothing for Quebec, Mr. Speaker. All they had last week was a cheque for $30,000 to plow under their potatoes, while their counterparts in the Atlantic provinces received compensation. And nobody from Quebec is standing up for them.
Mr. Speaker, at the GM plant in Boisbriand, they are still waiting to hear about the subsidies.
There is another matter that has been going on for some time, in the riding of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), and I am referring to the employees at Melcher's.
Then there is the famous promise concerning a banking centre in Montreal. It now looks as if we might have a counter to deposit cheques during the night, not to cash them! You read newspaper reports concerning the economic fall-out of the space station-Quebec was awarded only one contract while Ontario ended up with ten of them.
There is the matter of equalization payments.
In the immigration sector, the provincial government asked for financial compensation to be able to cope with the massive influx of refugees into Quebec, but again this Conservative Government said no.
Referring to Bill C-18 provisions related to railway transport, Minister Cote said that the impact will be felt in regions far from Montreal, services will be cut back. Again no answer, and no objections raised by Members.
I read an article today which clearly indicates that the Minister asked for funds to clean up the environment, just like Ontario got to fight pollution in the Great Lakes. Sure enough, we were told the Minister had left for Montreal and said: "No way, not a cent!"
Other files. Quotas in the footwear industry. The textile and clothing sector.
I am working on my 17th file concerning Quebec consumer associations still waiting for answers to their applications for grants to promote the interests of Quebecers.
Mr. Speaker, I have 17 files here which have been pending, unanswered. Talk about other files which were settled, Domtar to name one. Why did Domtar get money? Because we had to set up a survival committee to force the Government-and here I must pay homage to my colleagues from Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) and Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif) who were very active or. the Domtar survival committee-to award grants to Domtar. But this was not new money, it came from the funds given to the provincial government.
Let me get back to the matter of Montreal East. There was a survival committee made up of people from all political parties. You may recall that the Gulf refinery was shut down, but the Member for Mercier did not even lift a finger. Mr. Speaker, a Minister has resigned. A Conservative Member has crossed the floor, he is now an NDP Member and still nothing

has come from Ottawa. As in the other case, the Domtar case, the Provincial Government has obtained that half of the refining facilities remain in operation.
Canadair was taken over by Bombardier-the CF-18 contract. I know that in a few moments the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais), the Hon. Member for Hochelaga-Maisonneuve	(Mr. Desrosiers), the Hon.
Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine)-the three or four who were there today-will try to tell us that the obtained that. That is not true. It was Norm Cherry, the Canadair union representative, who set up a survival Committee, a pressure group, and enlisted all Montreal businessmen, all the church establishment. Although I admire wholeheartedly the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie and the sincerity and the persistance with which he pursues these issues, occasionally there is a hint of partisanship which also comes to the fore in his motion, and as a Member of the New Democratic Party, I must say that I find no reference to the third party in this House. Although the idea put forward today is rather new, one should wonder why, when they had the opportunity, the Liberal party of Canada and the Liberal party of Quebec never established such a mechanism as suggested by this motion.

Times may have changed or perhaps priorities. I would suggest to my honourable friends on the Government benches that it might have been a change with people which brought about a change in attitude and resulted in . .. It totally ignores the way our Parliamentary system works, under which, according to our Parliamentary tradition, the powers of Government are used by the executive. project will insure a long term viability to a great number of businesses using natural gas as the basis of their products. This is yet another achievement of our Government, which also means 250 additional jobs.

IMMIGRATION-SALVADORANS AND GUATEMALANS-REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION OF CANADA-UNITED STATES AGREEMENT. (B) PROCESSING OF REFUGEE STATUS APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very troubled that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Adjournment Debate
Bouchard) has done great harm to many refugees coming from the United States to Canada, particularly Salvadorans and Guatemalans. Because of his decision to send them back to the United States to wait for their inquiry in Canada, he has not only forced them to live for weeks and months in absolute poverty and in extreme anxiety through fear of being sent back to the country from which they fled, but he may in fact have caused them to be deported from the U.S. to El Salvador and Guatemala because when they are returned to the United States, they are arrested and charged with being illegal aliens.
This issue arises from a question I raised in the House on February 20 when the Minister made his announcement. On that day the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration told the House:
-Canada-and this dates back to some time-has an agreement with the United States of America which provides, particularly in this case, that people who apply for refugee status in Canada and whom we are unable to process immediately will not be deported by the United States.... We are exchanging correspondence, but I see no point in tabling documents today. I repeat, nobody has been deported by the United States, and I have been assured that none will be.
There was evidently a reason why the Minister was unwilling to table that correspondence. That reason was that the correspondence did not in fact take the position attributed to the United States by the Minister. In fact, that correspondence took a contrary position. Mr. Alan Nelson, the U.S. Commissioner of Immigration, wrote that correspondence to Mr. Joe Bissett, the Director of Immigration in Canada.
He said that district directors will, on a case-by-case basis, at their discretion, set a reasonable period of time for the alien to effect such a departure. He said that the arrangements between Canada and the United States would not cover certain cases of refugees, including those where the refugee was under a deportation order, had a criminal record or where there was derogatory information.
Another spokesperson for the U.S. Immigration amplified this position. He said that the U.S. will not bend its policy to protect refugees turned away from the Canadian border purely because they have a request from Canada.
The Minister said at the end of his answer that he had an assurance which in fact he either knew he did not have, or if he did not know that, he should have known. On February 26, I wrote to the Minister pointing out this information and suggested that one of two things must be true, either the Minister was aware that his statements were, so to speak, inoperative, or he was not aware of the correspondence. If he was aware of it, I suggested, the only honourable course would be for him to resign for misleading the House. If he was unaware, then he owed this House an apology as well as the resignation of his executive director, Mr. J. B. Bissett, who had received the letter from Mr. Nelson.
I have had no reply from the Minister of Employment and Immigration. However, we have had public nonsense from his front man, the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
March 5, 1987
Adjournment Debate
Weiner), who was quoted in the Montreal Gazette on Thursday, February 26, as claiming that the United States has a "model record" on human rights issues. How utterly false. The Minister of State for Immigration must know better. He has access to the facts of immigration and acceptance of refugees. He must know what he says about the United States is wildly untrue. In the matter of human rights for Salvadorans in the United States, the U.S. record is shameful. It deports them back to those lands of prisons, torture and murder with only a token nod to refugee claims. For example, between September 1985 and October 1986, the United States processed 2,183 refugee claims of Salvadorans and admitted only 55. That is only 2.5 per cent. It forced 6,047 back to El Salvador. Of 471 refugee claims by Guatemalans, it accepted only five, which is 1 per cent, and forced 3,502 back to Guatemala. Was that just? Not by Canadian standards.
During 1983 to 1984 Canada found that from 25 per cent to 59 per cent of Salvadoran refugee claimants were true refugees. At the very least that is 10 times the figure found in the United States. From 57 per cent to 70 per cent of Guatemalan claimants in Canada were found to be true refugees. In other words, the very lowest rate of acceptance in Canada is 10 times as high as the highest rate in the United States. Shame on the United States of America. Shame on the Minister of State for Immigration for calling that a model record. Shame on the Minister of Employment and Immigration for throwing many hundreds of Salvadorans and Guatemalans back to the United States. Shame on him for telling the House that he had been assured that they would not be deported to El Salvador and Guatemala when he has no such assurance.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have an opportunity to comment further the response of the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) to the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) on February 20, 1987.
I would like to tell the Hon. Member that the American authorities and a United Nations Commissioner have stated on several occasions since the implementation of the temporary control measures that, under the agreement between our two countries, claimants who are scheduled for a hearing in Canada will not be deported to their country of origin.
The representative of the High Commissioner for Refugees in Ottawa stated on March 3 that no refugee status claimant had been threatened with deportation from the United States since the implementation of the temporary control measures.
Canada has received assurances that no claimant staying in the United States would be the subject of a deportation order and that these people would not be denied access to the border.
We have also obtained assurances that those for whom an inquiry date has been set would be allowed to remain in the
United States in the meantime. In addition, the United Nations Commissioner has said that there is no indication that this agreement between Canada and the United States will not be respected.
We can therefore assert, Mr. Speaker, that no one is in any danger.
The Deputy Commissioner of the Inquiry Directorate in the United States Immigration and Naturalization Service said that the U.S. Government had informed the Canadian Government it would allow the people involved to remain in the United States until the day set for their inquiry in Canada.
Our policy is humane, Mr. Speaker. All applications from people seeking refugee status will be examined individually.
When a person is not facing deportation from the United States, we set a date for an inquiry and he or she will be allowed to stay in the U.S. until that date. Should the U.S. Immigration Service indicate that the person is under an expulsion order and will be deported very shortly, he or she will be allowed to enter Canada immediately to await the inquiry.
The Government believes that these provisions afford sufficient protection to claimants coming from countries where they might be endangered.
To answer the Hon. Member's question regarding the process of granting refugee status, I would like to remind him that the new rules put in place May 21st, 1986, were designed to exclude from the process people coming from countries on list B-l, because they were the most likely to get a favourable decision. In effect, they would have received permission from the Minister upon filing a claim in Canada. It is clear that increasing numbers of non-genuine refugees, even from these countries, have taken advantage of these provisions and the Government had no alternative but to return to the procedure in existence before May 21st, 1986.
Such a policy change appeared to us as the only way to adequately protect and accept, legally, the true refugees in Canada.

subtopic: AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY-ELIMINATION OF 9 PER CENT TARIFF ON AUTOMOBILE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES-GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) REQUEST FOR MAINTENANCE OF TARIFF DIFFERENTIAL
AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY-ELIMINATION OF 9 PER CENT TARIFF ON AUTOMOBILE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES-GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) REQUEST FOR MAINTENANCE OF TARIFF DIFFERENTIAL
speechtext:
In this discussion I am pursuing the questions that I directed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and which were answered by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). First, we are focusing on the automotive trade, and second what the consequences would be for automotive trade both in Canada and the United States if the duties which presently exist were eliminated as part of the broader free trade arrangement between the two countries.
March 5, 1987

I asked the Minister if he was prepared to commit himself to the maintenance of that 9 per cent tariff which presently exists between the two countries. The 9 per cent tariff has the effect of operating as a sanction with respect to the Auto Pact. Parts and automobiles that go back and forth across the border are not subject to the 9 per cent duty. The reason is that they meet the qualifications which are set out both on the Canadian side and the American side of the border. In particular, on the Canadian side of the border, they meet the 60 per cent Canadian value-added safeguards which were promised by letter by the various producing companies to the Canadian Government in 1965 at the start of the Auto Pact.
I must say that in my various exchanges on the subject of free trade with the Secretary of State for External Affairs, I have never received such complete non-answers as in this case. The Minister must have returned from a trip and been totally out of touch with what had been taking place, and had absolutely nothing constructive to say. I regret that the Minister took that course, because ordinarily he is a Minister for whom I have some respect.
However, what we are facing with respect to the automotive industry is an extremely serious crisis which is highlighted today by the fact that the auto trade figures have been released by the Canadian parts manufacturers. These figures indicate that the Canadian auto trade balance dropped between 1985 and 1986 by 72 per cent. Our deficit with Japan went up over 36 per cent to a total of $3.1 billion in deficit in auto trade with Japan. The deficit went up by over 12 per cent to $1.9 billion with Korea, and other countries.
Therefore, we face a shrinkage of what used to be quite a healthy surplus in this sector of our economy to a mere $310 million. This is very small when considering the total Canadian automotive trade was $68 billion in 1986.
The key point which these figures show is that we must defend our capacity in a world of changing patterns of production and a world of changing technology. We must defend our capacity as a relatively small country but a country that can produce automobiles quite successfully.
We must retain our capacity to protect the existence in Canada of important production facilities. In short, we must protect the production safeguards of the Auto Pact. We must also extend those production safeguards to the Korean and Japanese companies which are being established here.
This is why I moved a Private Member's Motion to have all parts of the auto industry in the country meeting the 60 per cent Canadian value-added content requirement. However, let me point out that the Government has had, right from the start of the discussions on the Canadian-United States free trade arrangements, warnings by its own bureaucrats in secret documents, of which we have received copies, indicating that if the tariffs were reduced, the safeguards would become inoperative.
Adjournment Debate
Let me quote specifically from Annex II which is labelled "secret" to a document entitled "A Canada-U.S. Free Trade Area Agreement". It reads as follows:
Unless the sector were excluded from its product coverage, a Canadian-United States free trade agreement would of course lead, after the transitional period, to the elimination of Canadian duties on vehicles and original equipment parts ...
In the absence of any other constraints, this would mean that automobile producers (as well as Canadian car dealers and consumers) would be able to import vehicles and ... parts duty free and in effect the Auto Pact's production safeguards would become inoperative.
That is precisely the point we were making in our question.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to respond to the Hon. Member who has raised, once again, the question of the treatment of automotive trade in the current bilateral negotiations with the United States. This time it is as a result of a response given in the House on February 17. While the question has been asked many times previously, and the answer has not changed, I will be pleased to restate the position of the Government for the benefit of my hon. colleague.
I believe our position with regard to automotive trade in the negotiations with the U.S. is quite clear, consistent, and reasonable. The Government has said repeatedly that the Auto Pact is working well, and that Canada would not be raising it at the table during the trade talks-"if it ain't broke, don't fix it".
In the meantime we have undertaken a fact-finding exercise with the United States on automotive issues. This was in no sense a negotiation, but an exchange of information on the situation and trends in the automotive industry.
The Auto Pact is not the only auto related issue, however. A substantial and increasing portion of North American automotive trade takes place outside the Auto Pact. In 1984 this amounted to $3.3 billion Canadian. We will have to consider how it would be affected by any comprehensive agreement we might strike with the United States.
Remembering also that the over-all aim of these negotiations is to achieve a trading arrangement as free as possible from all impediments to trade, we will of course want to negotiate issues such as tariffs, customs procedures, procurement, imports from third countries, duty remission programs, and subsidies on both sides of the border. These important matters could well affect trade on automotive products.
The position taken by the Government of Canada is that if the United States side has proposals to make which would be of benefit to Canada by enhancing Canadian employment, production, and trade, we will listen with interest.
